### Reviewer 1

In this study, Kempen et al. reported that IL-17A-IL-17RA signalling in Paneth cells is critical for host defence responses in the small intestine. The authors also revealed that IL-17A-induced Nox1 is necessary for the subsequent tissue regeneration responses mediated by ADAM17 enzymatic activity. To provide in vivo evidence to support their conclusions, the authors used a series of Paneth cell-specific knockout mice, including Il17rafl/fl Defa6-cre and Adam17fl/fl Defa6-cre. This study is likely to attract wide attention from scientists involved in mucosal immunology.
Overall, the observations and underlying implications described here are both reasonable and significant. The experiments are rigorous, with sufficient replicates and controls. However, it is well known that intestinal epithelial cells are a major IL-17A-targeting cell type in the gut, and that IL-17A is considered a protective cytokine at the mucosal surface because it can induce antibacterial peptides and work synergistically with IL-22. Therefore, these previous reports and existing knowledge compromise the novelty of the current study.
My only major concern about this study is that the authors only used Il17rafl/fl Defa6-cre mice to represent a genetic deficiency in IL-17A signalling in Paneth cells. However, IL-17RA is the receptor for all IL-17 family cytokines. IL-17RC deficiency is more relevant to claiming the specific effects of IL-17A/F. IL-17RA deficiency cannot rule out the effects mediated by IL-17C, since IL-17RA forms a heterodimer with IL-17RE in response to IL-17C, and IL-17C-IL-17RA/RE signalling has also been reported to play an important role in maintaining mucosal homeostasis. Therefore, the authors should rule out or include the effects of IL-17C in their study.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript “Immune cell-derived IL-17A promotes Paneth cell dedifferentiation through the Nox1-ADAM17 axis to regenerate the gut epithelium” by Kempen et al. describes a novel function of IL-17RA signaling in regulating the reprogramming of Paneth cells into multipotent stem-like cells upon irradiation. By selectively knocking out IL-17RA in Defa6-expressing Paneth cells, the authors provide evidence that Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA signaling protects against irradiation-induced intestinal damage.
Using Paneth cell lineage-tracing mice, they further show that Paneth cells can acquire stem cell–like features following intestinal injury, a process that can be blocked by neutralizing IL-17A with antibodies. Mechanistically, the study demonstrates that IL-17A increases ADAM17 expression in Paneth cells. Notably, Paneth cell–specific ADAM17 knockout phenocopied the IL-17RA knockout in the context of irradiation-induced injury, while ectopic ADAM17 expression rescued the effects of IL-17RA deficiency.
The manuscript also establishes a link between IL-17RA–dependent Nox1 expression, ROS production, and ROS-mediated ADAM17 activation. Pharmacological inhibition of ROS with NAC suppressed the dedifferentiation of Paneth cells into stem-like cells after irradiation, suggesting a central role for ROS in injury-induced Paneth cell plasticity. Finally, the authors indicate that ADAM17 promotes tissue regeneration primarily by enhancing cellular proliferation rather than by modulating gut barrier proteins.
The findings are highly exciting and of significant scientific interest, as they identify a novel function of IL-17RA signaling in regulating Paneth cell reprogramming during intestinal injury. It has become increasingly clear that Paneth cells play a central role in maintaining intestinal integrity—not only through their functions as innate immune cells and as stem cell niche supporters but also by serving as an alternative stem cell population that contributes to intestinal regeneration following tissue damage. While defects in Paneth cell function have long been associated with the development of intestinal inflammatory diseases, recent evidence shows that the reacquisition of stem cell features during inflammation can also enable Paneth cells to give rise to intestinal tumors (Verhagen et al., 2024 DOI: 10.1038/s41588-024-01801-y). In light of these diverse roles of Paneth cells in both health and disease, it is critical to better understand how their fate is extrinsically regulated.
Kempen et al. have invested considerable effort in studying the role of IL-17RA signaling in Paneth cells by employing several transgenic mouse lines and ex vivo organoid systems, providing strong support for a role of IL-17A signaling in regulating Paneth cell plasticity. Their findings may also have translational relevance, as they could open new avenues for the treatment of IBD or for supportive care during irradiation therapy. In this regard, the authors should consider performing additional experiments to broaden the translational impact of their study.
As IL-17RA signaling appears to be dispensable for Paneth cell dedifferentiation during DSS-induced gastroenteritis (Lin et al., 2022 DOI: 10.1016/j.immuni.2021.12.016), the mechanism described by Kempen et al. does not seem to be universal, but rather context-dependent and influenced by the type of injury. It would therefore be valuable to examine whether Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA signaling is also relevant for intestinal regeneration following chemotherapy, thereby expanding the potential scope of IL-17A–based supportive care.
Moreover, it would strengthen the study to assess whether a similar mechanism might apply to colonic regeneration. Recent findings indicate that Paneth-like Deep Crypt Secretory (DCS) cells in the colon can revert to stem-like cells to support tissue repair during colitis (Xu et al., 2025 DOI: 10.1038/s41418-025-01471-1). The authors could, for example, evaluate whether DCS proliferation is impaired in irradiated IEC-specific IL-17RA knockout mice (e.g. by co-staining PCNA or Ki67 with DCS markers such as Reg4, c-Kit, or WGA), or at least determine whether colonic damage is exacerbated upon epithelial loss of IL-17RA or blockade of IL-17A signaling with neutralizing antibodies. Demonstrating that IL-17RA signaling also contributes to colonic regeneration would substantially enhance the relevance of the study with relatively limited additional effort.
Beyond these points, I have additional critical remarks and questions that should be addressed prior to considering this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications. These points are summarized in bullet-point format for clarity:
1. First, and perhaps the most crucial experiment missing to convincingly demonstrate that IL-17RA directly regulates Paneth cell dedifferentiation, is the analysis of lineage tracing in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre;mTmG mice. I am somewhat surprised that the authors did not do this experiment. Although the anti-IL17A antibody treatment causes a reduction of Defa6-lineage tracing it might be due to other indirect mechanisms.
2. Likewise, irradiation-induced Paneth cell lineage tracing should be assessed in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre;mTmG mice. Alternatively, Paneth cell proliferation should be quantified by co-staining proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67 or PCNA) with Paneth cell–specific markers such as lysozyme to support the importance of ADAM17 for Paneth cell dedifferentiation.
3. As the authors introduce the depletion and re-appearance of canonical ISCs upon irradiation (Fig. 2B), they should address whether the regeneration of canonical ISCs is impaired in IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice (e.g. by a simple OLFM4 staining or Lgr5 in situ hybridization).
4. Kempen and colleagues claim increased intestinal damage in IL17RA whole-body knockout mice or in mice with IL17RA knockout in IECs. Although they demonstrate increased bacterial dissemination in the spleen and liver, the only reported evidence of enhanced tissue damage is a minor reduction in crypt length. Why did the authors not include additional parameters such as villus length, weight loss, quantification of viable crypts (as in Metcalfe et al., 2014 PMID: 24332836), or quantification of PCNA+ cells, as they performed in Fig. 3D for the Paneth cell–specific knockout? The same concern applies to the mice treated with IL17A antibodies (Figure 5) and the mice overexpressing ADAM17 (Figure 6). The inclusion of some additional parameters would provide stronger support for their claim.
5. In Figure 2C, the authors report reduced Lyz mRNA levels in the intestinal epithelium of IL17RA knockout mice after irradiation, which led them to further investigate IL17RA signaling in Paneth cells. However, it remains unclear whether this reduction is due to decreased lysozyme expression within Paneth cells or to a reduction in Paneth cell numbers upon loss of IL17RA. To address this, Paneth cells should be stained and quantified. Similarly, Paneth cell numbers and lysozyme expression should be evaluated in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice and IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, in order to determine whether a decrease in lysozyme expression can be also observed upon tissue or Paneth cell specific Il17RA knockout.
6. Regarding the effects on lysozyme expression upon IL17RA knockout, I have another critical remark: in their prior study (Lin et al., 2022 PMID: 35081371), the authors reported no difference of lysozyme expression in the intestinal epithelium of 6-week-old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice, while Paneth cell number was reduced in 10-week-old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice. In the current manuscript, the only information provided about mouse age is found in the Methods section, where it is stated that animals were between 6 and 15 weeks old. Given the previously described age-dependent effects of IL17RA deletion on Paneth cells, it is essential to indicate the exact age of the mice used in each experiment.
7. In Figure 4, the authors dedicate an entire section to different Paneth cell populations, mentioning a Defa6-low population, expressing stem cell genes. These cells likely represent Paneth cell progenitors, potentially more prone to dedifferentiate than Defa6-high/OLFM4-low cells. However, no experiments were performed to address this. For example, this could have been tested by analysing the organoid-forming capacity sorted Defa6-YFP high and low or Defa6-GFP high/CD24+ and Defa6-GFP low/CD24+ cells following irradiation. At minimum, the authors should discuss the possibility that the differentiation status of Paneth cells may influence their ability to dedifferentiate upon injury.
8. The authors show lineage tracing in Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice upon irradiation (Figure 5A) as well as organoid growth from sorted GFP+CD24+ cells from these mice (Figure 5B). However, no quantification is provided for the lineage tracing frequency (i.e. the number of tracings per GFP labelled crypt) between non-irradiated and irradiated mice, nor is there quantification of the number of GFP+ organoids per plated cells to indicate the efficiency of Paneth cells to dedifferentiate. In Figure 5D and Figure 6K, the authors do quantify single GFP+ cells and GFP+ clones in crypts and villi, but it is not explained how these quantifications were performed or what the y-axis represents. This information should be clarified.
9. In Figure 5G, the authors claim to provide evidence for increased Paneth cell lineage tracing in IL17A-treated organoids. I find this interpretation unconvincing: the images do not show ribbons of GFP+ cells that would indicate lineage tracing but rather single GFP+ cells distributed in organoid buddings, consistent with the normal localization of Paneth cells. A more likely explanation is that IL17A treatment enhances Paneth cell differentiation, similar to what they reported previously (Lin et al., 2022 PMID: 35081371). The authors might argue that organoid passaging results in fully GFP-labelled organoids; however, the images in Figures 5H and 5I are also not convincing in this regard. Instead, they appear more consistent with immature spheres, though this is difficult to assess because no bright-field images were provided to illustrate organoid morphology. Stronger evidence is needed to convincingly demonstrate Paneth cell dedifferentiation ex vivo.
10. The rationale behind the selection of genes analyzed in the context of Paneth cell dedifferentiation (Figure 6A) is not entirely clear. For example, why did the authors examine Wnt9b and Wnt6 to assess Wnt signaling rather than canonical Wnt target genes such as Axin2, CyclinD1, c-Myc, or CD44? Similarly, why were Dll1 and Dll4 measured instead of established Notch target genes such as HES or HEY to evaluate pathway activity? In addition, the authors did not include YAP target genes, despite their own re-analysis of scRNA-seq data showing that YAP targets are upregulated in the same Paneth cell subcluster with the highest expression of ADAM17 and Nox1 (Figure 6H). Likewise, in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, the authors measured expression of Hif1α, Hk2, Slc2a1, and Pgk1, but only Hif1α is discussed in the text. What was the rationale for including the other genes?
11. The title of the manuscript suggests that Paneth cell dedifferentiation is regulated through the NOX1–ADAM17 axis, which is a strong claim given that the only evidence indicating an involvement of NOX1 is the upregulation of NOX1 mRNA upon irradiation and IL-17A treatment, and the downregulation of NOX1 mRNA in irradiated ADAM17fl/fl; Defa6-Cre mice. At a minimum, effects on NOX1 expression should be confirmed at the protein level, ideally by immunostaining in mouse tissues. Additionally, demonstrating reduced ROS production upon Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA knockout (e.g., by ROS analysis in irradiated organoids using indicators such as CellROX or H2DCFDA) would further strengthen the proposed link between IL-17RA signaling and ROS-mediated ADAM17 activation. Even then, the title might falsely indicate regulation by NOX1, as ROS might be increased by multiple other mechanisms upon irradiation.
12. Regarding the title, I have an additional remark: the authors do not provide direct evidence that the observed effect is specifically mediated by immune cell–derived IL-17A. To be accurate, either immune cells should be removed from the title, or experiments should be included to specifically address their involvement. Notably, IL-17A can be expressed by other cell types, such as fibroblasts, as reported by Lotti et al., 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20131195).
13. As stated in the main text, ADAM17 is expressed in Paneth cells of both naïve and irradiated mice (Fig. S5A). Based on the images, ADAM17 expression appears to be considerably lower in irradiated mice compared to non-irradiated controls. The authors neither comment on this nor provide further analysis of differential ADAM17 expression between the two conditions. If confirmed, this would contradict the results shown in Figure 6H, where re-analysis of published scRNA-seq data from irradiated mice indicated increased ADAM17 expression. This discrepancy should be addressed and discussed.
14. Figure S6 is intended to show a Paneth cell–specific ADAM17 knockout; however, ADAM17 expression also appears reduced in other epithelial cells. Here either higher-quality images should be provided to clarify this or it should be commented on why a Paneth cell–specific knockout might lead to a broader reduction of ADAM17 expression.
15. Figure 6K shows a reduction of lineage tracing in NAC-treated mice. Is it possible to assess ADAM17 activity in these mice? This would help to strengthen the link between ROS production and ADAM17 activation.
16. Regarding Figure 7F, Kempen et al. state that there is no difference in the tight junction protein ZO-1 in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre mice and conclude that ADAM17 limits damage in response to irradiation by promoting cellular proliferation rather than modulating gut barrier proteins. However, based on the images provided in Figure 7F, it appears that ZO-1 is absent in the crypts of Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre mice. The authors should either reconsider their statement or provide additional data to support their interpretation.
In addition to the above I have some minor remarks:
1. In Figure 1A and F, Figure 3A, Figure 5E, Figure 6M, Figure 7A, Figure S3A it is not described what the arrows should indicate.
2. Y-axes in Figure 1A,, 3A, 5E, 6M, 7A, 7D should start from 0.
3. It is not described how PCNA+ cells in Figure 3D and Figure 7D were quantified (cells per crypt? How many crypts per mouse?)
4. Authors should describe in more detail how outliers were identified and in which experiments outliers were excluded.
5. It is not always clear how many times the experiments were repeated or how many samples were analyzed and quantified. For example, the authors state: “Figures 5A, 5B, 5G, and 5I are representative of 2–3 mice. Figures 5B, 5D, 5E, 5G, and 5H are generated from 2–3 independent experiments, and representative images are shown and quantified.” This level of reporting is insufficient for a high-quality journal such as Nature Communications. The exact number of biological and technical replicates, as well as the precise number of mice analyzed in each experiment, must be clearly specified.
6. The manuscript refers to Figure S6A, however, Figure S6 has no A or B.
Altogether, in my opinion considerable additional work is required for the manuscript to reach the high standard expected for Nature Communications. Nonetheless, I am confident that the authors can address the points raised, and that, with these revisions the manuscript could make a significant impact in the field.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Paneth cells and their antimicrobial products are critical in mediating small intestinal host defense under homeostatic conditions and after injury or infection. In addition, Paneth cells have also been shown to gain stem-like properties and repropagate intestinal crypts after intestinal injury. The specific role of intestinal IL-17A or its receptor (IL-17RA) signaling in Paneth cells to gain stem-like features has yet to be investigated. Using Paneth cell-specific IL-17RA (Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre) knockout mice, anti-IL-17A neutralizing studies and lineage tracer (Defa6-cre;mT/mG) mice, we show that after injury IL-17RA signaling is required for Paneth cell to gain stem-like properties to regenerate the intestinal epithelium. Increased susceptibility of Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice is associated with reduced expression Adam17 in the terminal ileum. Adam17 overexpression in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice rescues the epithelial regeneration defect in these mice. IL-17A induces Nox1 in Paneth cells and H O induces ADAM17 enzymatic activity. Finally, using Paneth cell-specific Adam17 (Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre) knockout mice, we show that ADAM17 in Paneth cells is required for tissue regeneration. Collectively, our data reveal an essential role of the IL-17RA-ADAM17 pathways in Paneth cells for tissue regeneration.

---

## Introduction

Paneth cells are highly specialized cells vital for regulating microbiota homeostasis, instituting protective antimicrobial processes, and providing a niche for developing stem cells (1–4). They are localized at the base of intestinal crypts. Patients with Crohn’s Disease (CD), a form of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), exhibit abnormalities and impaired antimicrobial processes within their Paneth cells (5). A hallmark of Paneth cells is their large, dense secretory granules. These granules store various antimicrobial peptides used to regulate the host microbiota and defend against invading pathogens (6–8). Paneth cells also play a vital role in maintaining the intestinal stem cell (ISC) niche. They produce epidermal growth factor (EGF) and selective WNTs, which help support the self-renewal and survival of Lgr5+ ISCs (2, 7). After intestinal injury, it has been reported that other intestinal epithelial cell types, including Paneth cells, can dedifferentiate and replenish the intestinal crypt (9–12). This process is dependent on the activation of multiple pathways. Notch signaling through notch intracellular domain (NICD) activation has been implicated in Paneth cell dedifferentiation and proliferation (10, 12). Simultaneously, it was reported that stem cell factor (SCF) signaling to c-Kit in response to inflammation causes Paneth cell dedifferentiation through activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling axis (9). While IL-17RA is expressed on the intestinal epithelium, including Paneth cells (13, 14), it is not known if immune cell-derived factors such as IL-17A regulate Paneth cell dedifferentiation.

The IL-17 family of cytokines is widely studied and plays an important role in immunity and inflammation (15). While the family consists of 6 signaling molecules (IL-17A-F), IL-17A and IL-25 (formerly known as IL-17E) are the best characterized (15, 16). IL-17A signals primarily through the IL-17RA/RC co-receptor complex. IL-17RA is expressed widely across mammalian tissue, while IL-17RC expression is restricted to epithelial, mesenchymal cells and few other cell types (17). Since IL-17A can signal to many cell types throughout the body, its expression and production are tightly controlled. Increased expression of IL-17A can be a contributing factor to autoimmune diseases, such as plaque psoriasis (18, 19). Increased amounts of IL-17A are also found in the intestinal mucosa of patients suffering from IBD (20). Anti-IL-17A or anti-IL-17RA therapies commonly used to treat plaque psoriasis patients were unsuccessful in treating IBD and, in some instances, worsened the disease (21, 22). We and others have shown that IL-17A is vital in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity after injury and promoting gut microbiota homeostasis (23–26). Recently, we have shown that IL-17A signaling within the gut, specifically to Lgr5+ stem cells, promotes secretory lineage commitment at a steady state (13). While a beneficial role for IL-17A signaling within the gut has been established, the role of IL-17A signaling to specific intestinal epithelial cell types is still an area of active research. After injury, several epithelial cell types, including Paneth cells, endocrine, and enterocytes, gain stem-like properties to regenerate the gut epithelium (9, 27, 28). Almost nothing is known at present whether IL-17A promotes or inhibits epithelial cell stem-like properties.

Our findings suggest that while, loss of IL-17RA signaling to Paneth cells is insignificant under homeostasis, however, the ability of Paneth cells to dedifferentiate and replenish the intestinal crypt after injury depends on IL-17RA. Utilizing our whole-body IL-17RA knockout (Il17raKO) and Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre mice, we show a lack of IL-17RA signaling to the intestinal epithelium leads to systemic bacterial dissemination to the spleen and liver after lethal doses of irradiation. This is compounded by significant structural damage and inflammation within the gut of these mice. This phenotype is recapitulated within our Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, showing the importance of IL-17RA signaling to Paneth cells in recovering from injury. Neutralizing IL-17A in irradiated Paneth cell lineage tracer (Defa6-cre;mT/mG) mice reduces stemness and epithelial regeneration. We show that continuous stimulation of organoids grown from Paneth cell lineage tracer mice with IL-17A increases the number of Paneth cells in organoid buds after irradiation. Furthermore, a subset of these Paneth cells gains stemlike properties and can develop into new organoids after passage. We found reduced expression of Adam17 in the terminal ileum of irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice. Furthermore, sorted Paneth cells from irradiated Paneth cell lineage tracer organoids treated with IL-17A showed increased expression of Adam17 and Nox1. NOX1 regulates epithelial redox, and H O enhances ADAM17 enzymatic activity. Using Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice, mechanistically, we show that epithelium, including Paneth cell-based, intestinal regeneration is linked to the IL-17A-ADAM17 axis.

---

## Results

Loss of intestinal IL-17RA signaling promotes intestinal bacterial dissemination to the spleen and liver.
Radiation injury is a well-established model to study Lgr5+ stem cell-independent epithelial regeneration as it ablates actively proliferating stem cells (27). C57BL/6 (WT) and whole-body IL-17RA knockout (Il17raKO) mice were irradiated at 12 Gy and returned to their cages. This dose of irradiation promotes intestinal epithelial cell damage and widespread death of Lgr5+ ISCs and transit-amplifying (TA) cells within crypts (29). Mice were sacrificed 5 days post-irradiation and tissues were collected. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of terminal ileal tissue from irradiated Il17raKO mice revealed greater structural damage and inflammation compared to WT mice. Specifically, we measured the length of the crypt/villi structure. We measured from the base of the crypt to the top of the villi and observed shortening of the crypt/villi structure in irradiated Il17raKO mice as compared to WT mice (Fig. 1A). Their liver and spleen were harvested, homogenized, and plated. After 48 hours, colonies were counted. We observed significant growth of bacterial colonies from spleen and liver tissues taken from Il17raKO mice when compared to tissues from WT mice (Fig. 1B). Along with this, there was increased Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) in the cecal contents of Il17raKO mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 1C). LCN2 is a siderophore known to help control microbiota dysbiosis and used as a marker for intestinal inflammation (30). While LCN2 can be induced by IL-17A, it can also be induced by a plethora of inflammatory stimuli (e.g., LPS) and cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-10, and IL-22) (31). To determine whether the loss of IL-17RA signaling affected proliferation within the intestinal villi, we performed immunofluorescence (IF) staining and stained tissue for proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA). Results showed reduced proliferation in the ileum of Il17raKO mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 1D). To rule out hematopoietic failure contribution to an observed phenotype, bone marrow from non-irradiated WT and Il17raKO mice were transplanted into their irradiated counterparts 2 hours post-irradiation (Fig. 1E). We observed a significant increase in systemic bacterial dissemination in Il17raKO mice compared to their WT counterparts (Fig. 1F). To further explore IL-17RA signaling within the intestines, we used intestinal epithelial-specific IL-17RA knock-out mice (Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre+/-). Irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre+ mice similarly showed greater structural damage and increased bacterial dissemination to the spleen and liver than their cre- counterparts (Fig. 1G & 1H). We also observed a trend towards increased LCN2 in the cecal content of irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre+ mice (Fig. 1I). Lastly, we also observed reduced cellular proliferation in the ileum of cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. 1J). Taken together, these observations show that lack of intestinal IL-17RA signaling resulted in gut barrier or epithelial regenerative defects.

Rapid depletion of Lgr5⁺ stem cells does not compromise intestinal regeneration following irradiation-induced injury.
A prior study showed that Lgr5+ cells are indispensable for tissue recovery after radiation-induced injury (32). It is also well established in the literature that radiation readily kills Lgr5+ stem cells (29, 33, 34). Utilizing Lgr5-EGFP-creERT2;RosaLSLTdtomato mice, we confirmed that radiation ablated Lgr5+ cells in the small intestine, which then reappear 7 days post irradiation (Fig. 2A & B). Once the involvement of Lgr5+ stem cells was ruled out, we then investigated which other cell type may mediate IL-17RA-induced protection. To do this, we screened for changes in RT-qPCR data from post-irradiated Il17raKO mice. Results revealed decreased expression of the Paneth cell marker Lyz1. We saw no differences in the expression of markers for other intestinal epithelial cells such as Muc2 (goblet cells), clusterin (Clu), a marker for a type of quiescent intestinal stem cells, and fetal-like markers including Anxa1, Anxa3, Anxa5, Ly6A, and Ly6D. (Fig. 2C). To confirm this expression data, we stained Il17raKO and Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre+ mice for Lyz1. We saw reduced amounts of Lyz1 in the ileum of both subsets of mice as compared to their WT and cre- counterparts (Fig. 2D & E). Since we observed decreased expression of Lyz1 in irradiated Il17raKO mice, followed by decreased amounts of Lyz1 in both Il17raKO and Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre+ mice, we decided to study the role of IL-17RA signaling in Paneth cells.

During homeostasis loss of IL-17RA signaling to Paneth cells does not alter their function.
To study the importance of IL-17RA signaling in Paneth cells, we generated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, which lack IL-17RA specifically on Paneth cells (Fig. S1A) (13). We extensively characterized naïve Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice. RNA-seq data from ileum tissues Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice showed no significant alterations in the expression of antimicrobial peptides or stem cell genes (Fig. S1B). To validate this data, we performed RT-qPCR of Paneth cell-related genes from ileum tissue of Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice, which did not show significant differences in expression between cre-/+ mice (Fig. S1C). Furthermore, IF staining for Lyz1 in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice showed no differences in the number of Lyz1+ Paneth cells (Fig. S1D). We show that Paneth cells of Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice display similar morphology and secretory vesicle number via transmission electron microscopy of ileal tissues (Fig. S1E). Acid Urea (AU) PAGE electrophoresis was performed to determine changes in cryptidin levels between Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice. AU-PAGE is a unique form of protein electrophoresis that separates proteins based on their charge. Results indicated no differences in cryptidin protein levels between cre- and cre+ mice (Fig. S1F). Lastly, 16S microbial sequencing revealed no changes in microbiota between naïve cre- and cre+ mice (Fig. S1G). Collectively, our data indicate that loss of IL-17RA signaling to Paneth cells does not alter their function under homeostatic conditions.

IL-17RA signaling, specifically to Paneth cells, promotes intestinal integrity after irradiation-induced injury.
We then characterized Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice after irradiation-induced injury. Our results were similar to those observed in Il17raKO and Il17rafl/fl;Villin-cre mice. There was shortening of crypt/villi length within the ileum of cre+ mice 3 days post irradiation (Fig. 3A). Five days post irradiation injury, there was increased bacterial dissemination to the spleen and liver in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. 3B). This was coupled with increased LCN2 concentrations within cre+ cecal contents (Fig. 3C). Utilizing an anaerobic chamber, we also observed increased anaerobic bacterial dissemination to the spleen and liver in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice (Fig. S1H). The presence of cecal albumin was indicative of gut barrier injury (Fig. S1I). Immunofluorescence staining of PCNA revealed decreased cellular proliferation in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice compared to cre- mice post-irradiation injury (Fig. 3D). We next wanted to determine if the regeneration canonical ISCs was impaired in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice after irradiation. As expected, we saw reduced amounts of Olfm4+ crypts in mice 5 days post irradiation as compared to non irradiated mice. Interestingly, we also observed decreased amounts of Olfm4+ crypts in irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as compared to irradiated cre- mice. This revealed that canonical ISCs regeneration was indeed impaired in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice 5 days post irradiation (Fig. 3E). We did not observe a difference in the number of Lyz1+ Paneth cells between cre- and cre+ mice post irradiation (Fig. S1J). Immune profiling revealed a lack of differences between populations of adaptive immune cells in the lamina propria of irradiated cre- and cre+ mice (Fig. S2A). However, total cell numbers of ILC1s were significantly greater in the lamina propria of irradiated cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. S2B). We also show that there are equivalent amounts of IL-17A producing ILC3s and CD3+ cells within the lamina propria of irradiated cre- and cre+ mice (Fig. S2C & S2D). Furthermore, there was no difference in key IL-17A inducible chemokine (Cxcl5, Ccl2 and Cxcl1) expression within the ilea of irradiated cre- and cre+ mice (Fig. S2E). Commensal microbiota have been shown to promote intestinal regeneration (35). Subsets of commensal microbiota expand at sites of intestinal injury and promote wound healing (36). We first compared the Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice microbiota in the non-irradiated control group. When observing beta diversity at the phylum, family, genus, and species level, there was no distinct clustering between groups. This indicates that with the Weighted UniFrac metric these groups are more similar than dissimilar at each phylogenetic level. Further, when performing LEfSe, no phylum, family, genus, or species were identified as significantly different in abundance between the cre+/- non-irradiated mice, even with an LDA cut-off of 1, and a p-value of 0.10 (Fig. 3F-I). While the microbiota composition changed after irradiation, the difference was subtle for both cre- and cre+ mice (Fig. 3J-M). These results suggest that IL-17RA signaling to Paneth cells is vital in limiting damage in response to irradiation independent of microbiota regulation.

Subsets of Paneth progenitors express high levels of IL-17RA and IL-17RC.
We have previously shown via single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) of enteroids that a small subset of Paneth cells expresses IL-17RA, while secretory progenitors express the highest levels of IL-17RA (13). To investigate this deeper, we analyzed a previously published single-cell RNA sequencing data set enriched for primary murine Paneth cells (PMID: 29144463), which identified three distinct subsets of Paneth cells (Paneth 1, Paneth 2, Paneth Progenitor) (14). The analysis of these data suggested no significant difference in the average level of IL-17RA expression over the course of Paneth cell differentiation, while IL-17RC expression decreased as Paneth cells matured (Fig. 4A). A more detailed analysis, however, demonstrated unique subsets of Paneth progenitors characterized by intermediate levels of Lyz1 and high expression of IL-17RA (Fig 4B) or IL-17RC (Fig 4C), consistent with our previous results. Utilizing PanethYFP (Defa6-cre;YFP) mice, we were able to show two distinct Paneth cell populations. The high YFP-positive cells represent matured Paneth cells, and cells expressing low levels of YFP mark Paneth progenitors (Fig. 4D). RT-qPCR analysis of these two populations was consistent with previous results (Fig. 4B & 4C), demonstrating that low YFP expressing Paneth cells expressed higher levels of Il17rc, Il17ra, and Olfm4 (a marker for stemness) (Fig. 4E). Interestingly, we analyzed a previously published single-cell RNA sequencing data (PMID: 29887318) which showed that Il17rc and Il17ra are upregulated in Paneth cells after irradiation (Fig. 4F) (10). Taken together, we show that Paneth progenitors, a subset of Paneth cells, express high levels of Il17ra, Il17rc and stem cell markers. Furthermore, post irradiation Paneth cells express higher levels of Il17ra and Il17rc.

IL-17RA signaling promotes Paneth cell stemness after irradiation injury.
To better understand the mechanism by which Paneth cells participate in the regeneration of the intestinal crypt after irradiation-induced injury, we generated and validated Paneth cell lineage tracer mice (Defa6-cre;mT/mG). All Paneth cells and their lineage in these mice express GFP, while all other cells express RFP. Consistent with published literature (9, 10), we were able to show that Paneth cells gain stemness post-irradiation, as revealed by the appearance and counting of ribbons of GFP+ cells in the villus 5 days post irradiation (Fig. 5A). Immunofluorescence staining for GFP and MUC2 (goblet cell-specific marker) or DCLK1 (Tuft cell marker) or ChGA (enteroendocrine cell marker), or I-FABP (enterocyte cell marker) in these mice showed co-staining of GFP and these distinct cell markers, which supports the assertion that Paneth cells can dedifferentiate and repair/regenerate the intestinal crypt (Fig. 5A and S3A, respectively). Small intestinal crypt from non-irradiated Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice forms a viable organoid (Fig. 5B top panel). We next sorted GFP+CD24+ Paneth cells from non-irradiated and irradiated Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice. Non-irradiated sorted GFP+CD24+ Paneth cells do not form organoid. Green organoids (indicating organoids arising from Paneth cell lineage) only grew from Paneth cells sorted from irradiated mice (Fig. 5B bottom panel). To confirm the importance of IL-17A signaling in modulating Paneth cell stemness, we injected Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice with anti-IL-17A or IgG antibody, on day 0 and day 2 post irradiation (Fig. 5C). We then counted the number of GFP+ cells in the base of the crypt and in the villi between the two treatment groups 5 days post irradiation. We also counted the number of GFP+ clones, which we define as at least 4 GFP+ cells in a row, in the villi between the two treatment groups 5 days post irradiation. The results showed decreased GFP+ cells and clones in the villi of mice treated with anti-IL-17A as compared to IgG-treated mice (Fig. 5D). Furthermore, there was decreased crypt/villi length indicating structural damage in the terminal ilea of mice treated with anti-IL-17A compared to IgG treated mice (Fig. 5E). We also observed reduced proliferation in the ileum of mice treated with anti-IL-17A as compared to IgG-treated mice (Fig. 5F). This result demonstrates a strong connection between IL-17A signaling and Paneth cells ability to dedifferentiate and repair the intestinal crypt after radiation injury. We then established an organoid irradiation and regeneration model and identified that 6 Gy is an optimal dose of irradiation (Fig. S3B). Prior literature has also shown that doses lower than 6 Gy show minimal effects on organoid growth, while at 6 Gy, the initial loss of organoid budding was followed by renewed organoid regeneration (37). To confirm the importance of IL-17A in the regeneration of the intestinal epithelium, we supplied external recombinant IL-17A to organoids grown from Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice post-irradiation and observed increased GFP+ cells after IL-17A treatment (Fig. 5G & H). We have previously reported that IL-17A signaling on ISCs promotes secretory lineage commitment (13). Thus, the increased GFP+ cells we observe after IL-17A treatment may be increased amounts of mature Paneth cells or stem-like Paneth cells. To confirm presence of stem-like Paneth cells, we passaged these organoids and observed if any fully green organoids grew. Interestingly, when these organoids were passaged, we saw a higher percentage of fully green organoids from the wells that were treated with IL-17A, indicating that IL-17A may directly increase Paneth cell stemness after irradiation (Fig. 5I). Since IL-25 and IL-17C also signal through IL-17RA, we tested whether recombinant IL-25 or IL-17C can induce green organoids after irradiation. Our results showed no significant increase in green organoid development from passaged Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice post-irradiation after IL-25 or IL-17C treatment (Fig. S3C). We then stained the IL-17A treated green organoids for MUC2 and ChGA. MUC2 marks terminally differentiated goblet cells while ChGA marks terminally differentiated enteroendocrine cells. Since the staining revealed that these green organoids were composed of both GFP+/MUC2+ double positive cells and GFP+/ChGA+ double positive cells, we can ascertain that these green organoids arise from Paneth cells and are mature organoids composed of terminally differentiated epithelial cells (Fig. 5J). Collectively, our data show that IL-17A promotes Paneth cell dedifferention.

Overexpression of Adam17 rescued intestinal regeneration defect in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice after radiation-induced injury independent of EGFR ligands.
We next investigated mechanisms of IL-17A-induced Paneth cell stem-like properties. We performed RT-qPCR analysis in the terminal ileum of Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre mice for a range of genes involved in tissue regeneration pathways. These genes were selected because epithelial regeneration has been shown to be mediated via WNT, ADAM17, and Notch pathways (9, 38, 39) . Furthermore, the annexin family genes (Anxa 1, Anxa3, Anxa5), Ly6 family genes (Ly6a and Ly6d) and YAP family genes (Yap and Hbegf) are markers for the fetal-like reversion regenerative pathway (40–42). We showed decreased expression of Adam17, Dll1, and Wnt9b in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice after radiation injury compared to cre- mice. Interestingly, Ly6a but not Ly6d, Anxa1, Anxa3, Anxa5, Yap, and Hbegf expression was increased in the small intestine of cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. 6A & S4A). The increased expression of Ly6a may be occurring as an alternate regenerative mechanism to compensate for the decrease in expression of Adam17, Dll1, and Wnt9b after injury. The increased ligand expression of Ly6a does not appear to result in noticeable down stream effects. We also grew organoids from our Paneth cell lineage tracer mice and irradiated them for 24 hours as described prior. Next, we treated these organoids with IL-17A for 4 hours and sorted Paneth cells (Fig. 6B & S3D). RT-qPCR analysis of the sorted Paneth cells showed that 4 hour treatment of IL-17A directly increased the expression of Adam17, specifically in Paneth cells (Fig. 6C). ADAM17 is a metalloprotease involved in the proteolysis of ~80 proteins. Loss of ADAM17 has been shown to cause intestinal regenerative defects and is associated with chronic intestinal injury (39, 43, 44). Increased degradation of ADAM17 has also been shown to cause hair follicle stem cell exhaustion due to reduced Notch signaling (45). Hif1 has been shown to promote Adam17 expression (46, 47). Thus, we explored if the expression of Hif1 and its target genes (Hk2, Slc2a1, Pgk1) were also reduced in in the terminal ileum of irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice. No difference in expression was observed (Fig. 6D). Furthermore, RNA sequencing data (PMID: 29887318) also showed no difference in the expression of Hif1 related genes in Paneth cells post irradiation (Fig. 6E) (10). ADAM17 has also been shown to be modulated via NADPH oxidase 1 (Nox1). Specifically, the stability of ADAM17 has been shown to be mediated through Nox1. Nox1 has been shown to protect ADAM17 from ubiquitin-mediated degradation through direct interactions (48). Nox1 is also an important producer of intestinal epithelial ROS. Depletion of Nox1 significantly reduces intestinal epithelial ROS production (49). Oxidative stress and redox agents have been shown to activate ADAM17 and induce shedding of ADAM17 targets (50, 51). Thus, we explored if Nox1 may play a role in our observations. Expression of Nox1 was reduced in both naïve and irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ as compared to cre- mice, while expression patterns of other proliferative pathway genes remained unchanged between naïve Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ and cre- mice (Fig. S1K & Fig. 6F). Furthermore, immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining for Nox1 showed decreased Nox1 protein amounts in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ as compared to cre- post irradiation (Fig. S4B). RT-qPCR analysis of the sorted Paneth cells showed that 4 hour treatment of IL-17A also directly increased expression of Nox1 specifically in Paneth cells (Fig. 6G). Analysis of a previously published single cell RNA sequencing data (PMID: 29887318) also showed increased expression of Adam17, Nox1, and Olfm4 in Paneth cells post irradiation (Fig. 6H) (10). Since Nox1 is a major producer of ROS, we next show that exogenous redox agents such as H O is able to directly induce ADAM17 activity (Fig. 6I). To confirm the importance of ROS in modulating Paneth cell stemness, we gave Paneth cell lineage tracer mice 4% n-acetylcysteine (NAC) in their drinking water after irradiation (52). NAC is an antioxidant, which has been shown to be readily metabolized within the small intestine (53). Mice were kept on 4% NAC water until euthanasia 5 days post irradiation (Fig. 6J). We then quantified the number of GFP+ cells in the crypt and villi between the two treatment groups. The results showed decreased GFP+ cells and clones in the villi of mice given on 4% NAC water as compared to mice given untreated water (Fig. 6K). We also observed a trend towards decreased ADAM17 activity in the ileum of mice given on 4% NAC water as compared to mice given untreated water (Fig. S4C). Next, to study the role of ADAM17 in our observations, we utilized an ADAM17 adenovirus (Ad-Adam17) to overexpress Adam17 (Fig 6L & Fig. S4D). Overexpression of ADAM17 rescued Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice from structural damage as well, while not affecting Paneth cell number (Fig. 6M & Fig. S4E). Increased cellular proliferation was observed in the ileum of Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ after over expression of ADAM17 (Fig 6N). Overexpression of ADAM17 in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ showed reduced bacterial burden in their liver post irradiation injury (Fig. 6O). This was coupled with a trend towards decreased cecal LCN2 in these mice as well (Fig. S4F). Collectively, our data show that ADAM17 is required for intestinal epithelial regeneration.

ADAM17 expression in Paneth cells contributes to intestinal regeneration after radiation-induced injury.
We confirmed that both naïve and irradiated Paneth cells express ADAM17 by immunostaining the terminal ileum of control and irradiated Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice (Fig. S5A & S5B). We next generated Paneth (Defa6) cell-specific Adam17 knockout mice. Reduced staining of ADAM17 in Paneth cells in the ilea of Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice confirmed the specificity of the deletion (Fig. S6). We then irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice. Five days after irradiation Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice had greater structural damage than their cre- counterparts (Fig. 7A). We also observed increased cecal LCN2 and increased hepatic and splenic bacterial dissemination in irradiated cre+ mice (Fig. 7B & 7C). Irradiated cre+ mice also had reduced proliferation as compared to their cre- counterparts (Fig. 7D). To determine whether ADAM17 expression on Paneth cells was important for Paneth cell specific proliferation, we stained irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice for PCNA and Lyz1. We saw decreased amounts of proliferating Paneth cells in irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. 7E). While Paneth cell specific proliferation was decreased in Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+, overall proliferation remains was not effected. The intestinal epithelium has been shown to have high plasticity where a wide variety of epithelial cells can dedifferentiate to regenerate the epithelium in the absence of ISCs (28, 54). Thus, we believe if Paneth cell dedifferentiation is inhibited, other cell types would then help regenerate the intestine. While RT-qPCR analysis of regenerative markers within the terminal ileum yielded no significant differences between irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice, we did see a strong trend towards decreased Nox1 expression in Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice (Fig. 7F). To validate these finding, we stained for Nox1 in the ileum of irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice. Indeed, we saw decreased Nox1+ crypts/villi in Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. 7G). Nox1 has been show to stabilize and promote ADAM17 activation, which in turn can then activate the EGFR-ERK1/2 pathway. (48, 55, 56). The EGFR-ERK1/2 pathway modulates ATF-1 which has been shown to promote NOX1 signaling (57). Thus, Adam17 expression and Nox1 expression may result from a positive feedback loop and rely upon each other. We next wanted to determine if Paneth cell specific ADAM17 played a role in intestinal epithelial barrier integrity. First, we stained for ZO-1, a common epithelial cell tight junction protein, in the terminal ilea of irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ and cre- mice. We then looked at expression levels of two other tight junction proteins, Ocln and Cldn4, in the ilea of these mice. There was no difference in gap junction protein amounts or expression between Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre+ and cre- mice post irradiation (Fig. 7H & Fig. 7I). Taken together, these results show that Paneth cell specific ADAM17 signaling is vital in limiting damage in response to irradiation via promoting cellular proliferation rather than modulating gut barrier proteins.
