## Methods

Study Design
Animal studies were conducted with the approval and under all relevant ethical regulations of Stony Brook University's Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC protocol number 968871). The objective of this study was to determine the significance of IL-17RA signaling to Paneth cells in response to irradiation induced injury. Various genetically modified mice were utilized for this study. An irradiation-based injury model was utilized to study morphological, immunological, and regenerative changes within the small intestine. Sample sizes and replicates used were based on prior literature and experience with various tissue Il17ra knockout mice (12,13). Euthanasia time points were determined based on prior literature (34).

Mice
C57BL/6 (WT), Villin-Cre (C57BL/6 background), Gt(ROSA)26Sortm1(EYFP)Cos/J (C57BL/6 background) and ROSAmT/mG (C57BL/6 background) mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. Il17RAKO mice were obtained from Dr. Jay Kolls, Tulane University. Defa6-Cre mice were obtained from Dr. Richard Blumberg, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard. Lgr5-EGFP-creERT2 , Lgr5-EGFP-creERT2;RosaLSLTdtomato and Villin-creERT2 mice were obtained from Dr. Vincent W. Yang, Stony Brook University. Adam17fl/fl mice were obtained from Dr. Rebecca K. Martin, Virginia Commonwealth University. Generation and characterization of IL-17-Floxed (Il17rafl/fl) mice were performed as previously described (26). Il17rafl/fl mice were bred with Villin-Cre or Defa6-Cre to develop entire gut epithelium and Paneth cell specific IL-17RA knockout mice. Defa6-Cre mice were bred with Gt(ROSA)26Sortm1(EYFP)Cos/J or ROSAmT/mG mice to develop PanethYFP and Paneth cell lineage tracing mice, respectively. Adam17fl/fl mice were bred with Defa6-Cre mice to develop Paneth cell specific ADAM17 knockout mice. Mice of both genders were used for all experiments unless indicated in the figures. Mice ages for each experiment are provided in the figure legends. Littermate controls were used for experiments, thus all cre- and cre+ mice were age matched. Sex was not considered in this study design and analysis as it was not relevant to our findings. All mice were housed in specific pathogen-free conditions at Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY. All animal studies were conducted with the approval of Stony Brook University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

Animal Treatment
Anti-17A or IgG control (250g/mouse) was administered intraperitoneally to mice on same day of irradiation and 2 days post irradiation for select experiments. Mice were given 4% n-acetylcysteine in their drinking water directly after irradiation continuously until euthanasia on day 5 post irradiation for select experiments.

Cell Lines and Organoid Cultures
L-WRN cell line was obtained from Dr. Thaddeus Stappenbeck, Washington University. HEK-293 cell line was obtained from Dr. Vincent W. Yang, Stony Brook University.

Irradiation Treatment
Mice were irradiated at 12 Gy in a gamma cell irradiator (GammaCell 40; AEC Ltd). WT (C57BL/6) and Il17raKO mice bedding was mixed 1 week prior to gamma-irradiation to help ensure mixing of gut microbiota. Mice were euthanized at various time points (3 and 5 days) post irradiation and tissue was collected for experiments. Organoids were initially irradiated at increasing doses of gamma cell irradiation in a gamma cell irradiator (GammaCell 40; AEC Ltd) to develop our model. Once we confirmed 6 Gy as our optimal dose, all successive organoids were irradiated at 6 Gy. Organoids were then imaged and collected for RT-qPCR varying days post irradiation (3, 5, 6 days).

Bacterial Dissemination
Mice were euthanized 5 days post irradiation and their livers and spleens were harvested, weighed, homogenized, and plated on Luria broth (LB) or brain heart infusion (BHI) plates. After 48 hours, colonies were counted. Homogenates were also incubated in an anaerobic chamber (GasPak anaerobic container) for 48 hours and then counted to determine the dissemination of anaerobic bacteria.

Bone Marrow Transplantation
Wild type (WT) and Il17raKO mice were irradiated at 12 Gy. Non-irradiated WT and Il17raKO mice were euthanized and bone marrow was extracted from their femurs. Extracted bone marrow was then transplanted into their irradiated counterparts 2 hours post irradiation (1 million cells). Mice were then euthanized 5 days post irradiation and livers and spleens were harvested to measure bacterial dissemination as previously described and mesenteric lymph node was isolated for flow cytometry to ensure transplantation.

Induction of gene knockouts
To induce the knockout of genes, tamoxifen (1 mg/mouse) was administered intraperitoneally from day 0 to day 5 to Lgr5-EGFP-creERT2;RosaLSLTdtomato mice. On day 5 mice were irradiated and euthanized at multiple time points and tissues were harvested for bacterial dissemination.

Crypt Isolation
Ileums were harvested and flushed with ice-cold 1x PBS. They were then cut open longitudinally and Peyer’s patches were removed and cut into ~2 cm sections. Tissues were then washed in 30 mL of ice cold 1x PBS 3 times. Tissues were then incubated in 1x ice-cold PBS supplemented with 3.75 mM EDTA on an orbital rocket (60 rpm) for 30 minutes at 4C. Tissues were then washed twice with 50 mL of 1x ice-cold PBS. Tissues were then moderately shaken in 25 mL of ice cold 1x PBS and filtered through 70 micron filters to extract crypts. This was repeated three times to maximize crypt accumulation.

Organoid Culture
Isolate crypts were pelleted (300 x g) and re-suspended in Matrigel Matrix (Corning) at a concentration of ~100 crypts per 30 L Matrigel Matrix. 24 well plates were then seeded with 30 L/well of crypt suspension. The seeded plates were then incubated at 37C, 5% CO for 15 minutes to allow for Matrigel polymerization. The polymerized domes were then immersed in 500 L of enriched organoid growth medium (1:1 mixture of L-WRN and DMEM/F12) containing 1x penicillin-streptomycin-glutamine (Invitrogen), 1x B27 (Invitrogen), 1x N2 (Invitrogen), 50 ng/mL of murine EGF (R&D system), 1 mM of N-acetylcysteine (Sigma-Aldrich), 10 nM of Gastrin-Leu15 (Sigma-Aldrich), 500 nM of A83-01 (Torics), 10 mM of Y-27632 (Sigma-Aldrich) and 10 mM of CHIR99021 (Tocris). After 2 days, enriched organoid growth medium was replaced with supplemented organoid growth medium (no Y-27632 and CHIR99021). Supplemented organoid growth medium was continuously replaced every 2 days. Organoids were treated with IL-17A (50 ng/ml) every 2 days and harvested on day 6 for RT-PCR. Images were taken on days represented in figures with an Olympus CKX41 microscope.

For passaging, organoids were lifted in 500 L of cell recovery solution and incubated on an orbital shaker for 5 minutes at room temperature. Organoids were then pelleted (300g) and incubated in TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher) for 5 minutes to make a single cell solution. Cells were then resuspended in Matrigel Matrix and plated in a 24 well plate (30 L/well). Domes were then resuspended in enriched organoid growth medium and cultured as described above.

RT-qPCR
RNA was extracted from terminal ileum tissues via Trizol-based extraction or from organoids via RNeasy Mini Kit (QIAGEN). RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using Bio-Rad iScript kits according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RT-PCR was performed by mixing 5 L of SsoAdvanced Universal Probes Supermix (Bio-Rad) or SsoAdvanced Universal SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad), 4.5 L of cDNA and 0.5 L of primer per reaction. All analysis were done relative to Gapdh or Hprt. Primer sequences can be found in Supplemental Table S1.

ELISA
Cecal samples were collected from mice and stored at -80C until needed. Samples were prepared for ELISA as previously reported (68). Briefly, frozen cecal samples were thawed and homogenized in PBS containing 0.1% Tween 20 at a concentration of 100 mg/mL. Homogenates were then centrifuged for 10 minutes and 12,000 rpm to remove solid debris. Clear supernatant was collected and utilized for experimentation with Mouse Lipocalin-2/NGAL DuoSet ELISA kit (R&D Systems) or Mouse Albumin ELISA Kit (RayBiotech) as per manufacture’s protocol.
Tissue samples were collected, immediately flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80C until needed. Samples were homogenized for ELISA in tissue protein extraction buffer containing 100mM Tris (pH 7.4), 150mM NaCl, 1mM EDTA, 1% triton, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 1x protease inhibitor, phosphate inhibitor, and 1mM Phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF). Homogenates were then centrifuged at 17,000 x g for 20 minutes at 4C and clear supernatant was collected. Protein concentration was determined via Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kits (23225). Equivalent amounts of protein was the utilized for experimentation with Mouse Epiregulin ELISA Kit (RayBiotech) as per manufacture’s protocol.

Histopathology
Terminal ileum tissue samples were prepared into Swiss roles, fixed in 10% formalin overnight and embedded in paraffin blocks. Paraffin embedded blocks were cut into 5 micron sections and adhered onto charged slides. Samples were then deparaffinized via Xylene and rehydrated via a descending ethanol gradient (100%, 95%, 70%, pure dH2O). For hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, tissues were submerged in hematoxylin (VWR) for 5 minutes. Slides were then submerged in 3% acetic acid for 1 minute. Slides were then washed under running tap water for approximated 15 minutes. Tissues were then submerged in eosin (VWR) for approximately 1 minute. Slides were then submerged in 95% and 100% ethanol successively for 2 minutes. Slides were then mounted using toluene and imaged using an Olympus CKX41 microscope. Crypt lengths were measured via the program ImageJ.

Immunofluorescence
Terminal ileum tissue samples were prepared into Swiss roles, fixed in 10% formalin overnight and embedded in paraffin blocks. Paraffin embedded blocks were cut into 5 micron sections and adhered onto charged slides. Samples were then deparaffinized via Xylene and rehydrated via a descending ethanol gradient (100%, 95%, 70%, pure dH2O). Antigen retrieval was performed by heating slides in a steamer for 40 minutes. Tissues were then submerged under 1x PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) for 10 minutes and then washed three times with 1X PBS containing 0.01% Tween 20 (VWR) to be permeabilized. Tissued were then blocked by 1x PBS containing 5% fetal bovine serum at 34C for 1 hour. Following blocking, tissues were submerged in 1x PBS containing 5% fetal bovine serum with primary anti-bodies against LYZ1-FITC (1:200) (Dako: F037201), PCNA (1:200) (Santa Cruz: sc-56), GFP (1:100) (Cell Signaling: 295SS), MUC2 (1:200) (Abcam: ab272692), DCLK1 (1:200) (Cell Signaling: 62257S), ADAM17 (1:200) (Invitrogen: MA5-32572), RFP (1:200) (Rockland: 200-101-379), UEA1-Dylight 649 (1:200) (Vector: DL-1068), IL-17RA (1:200) (Abcam: ab180904), ChGA (1:200) (Santa Cruz: sc-393941), I-FABP (1:200) (Santa Cruz: sc-374482) and ZO-1 (1:200) (Invitrogen: 61-7300) at 4C overnight. The next day, slides were washed three times with 1x PBS, the sections were incubated for 30 minutes at room temperature with Alexa Fluor® 488 AffiniPure™ Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L) (1:200) (Jackson ImmunoResearch: 111-545-144), Alexa Fluor® 647 AffiniPure™ F(ab')₂ Fragment Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L)(1:200) (Jackson ImmunoResearch: 111-606-144), Alexa Fluor® 488 AffiniPure™ F(ab')₂ Fragment Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (H+L) (1:200) (Jackson ImmunoResearch: 115-546-003), or Alexa Fluor® 647 AffiniPure™ F(ab')₂ Fragment Donkey Anti-Goat IgG (H+L) (1:200) (Jackson ImmunoResearch: 705-606-147). Slides were then mounted with DAPI hard mount (Southern Biotech) and images were acquired using an Olympus CKX41 microscope.

Organoids were lifted using ice cold 1X PBS. Organoids were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 minutes. Organoids were then washed with 1X PBS and permeabilized with .01% triton in 1X PBS for 10 minutes. After permeabilization, organoids were washed with 1X PBS and then blocked in 1X PBS containing 5% BSA for 1 hour at 34C. After blocking, organoids were incubated overnight at 4C in 1X PBS containing 5% BSA with primary antibodies against GFP (1:100) (Rockland: 600-901-215), Muc2 (1:200) (Santa Cruz: sc-515032), or ChGA (1:200) (Santa Cruz: sc-393941). The next day, organoids were washed with 1X PBS and then incubated for 30 minutes at 37C in 1X PBS containing 5% BSA with secondary antibodies Alexa Fluor® 488 AffiniPure™ F(ab')₂ Fragment Donkey Anti-Chicken IgG (H+L) (1:100) (Jackson ImmunoResearch: 703-544-155) and Alexa Fluor® 647 AffiniPure™ F(ab')₂ Fragment Donkey Anti-Mouse IgG (H+L) (1:200) (Jackson ImmunoResearch: 715-605-150). Organoids were then washed with 1X PBS and mounted on slides with DAPI hard mount (Southern Biotech) and images were acquired using an Olympus CKX41 microscope.

Live fluorescent murine organoids endogenously expressed fluorescence and thus were directly imaged in culture using an EVOS M5000 imaging system.

Immunohistochemistry
Paraffin embedded blocks were cut into 5 micron sections and adhered onto charged slides. Samples were then deparaffinized via Xylene and rehydrated via a descending ethanol gradient (100%, 95%, 70%, pure dH2O). Antigen retrieval was performed by heating slides in a steamer for 40 minutes. Tissues were then incubated in hydrogen peroxide block (abcam: 58661) for 10 minutes at room temperature. Sections were then washed in MilliQ water 2 times for 5 minutes followed by 1 wash in 1X TBS-T for 5 minutes. Sections were then blocked for 1 hour at room temperature in 5% BSA in 1X TBS-T. Sections were then washed and avidin biotin block was performed as per manufacturers protocol (Vector: SP-2001). Sections were then incubated overnight at 4C in 1X TBS-T containing primary antibody against Nox1 (1:250) (Proteintech: 17772-1-AP). The next day, section were washed 3 times in 1X TBS-T. Sections were then incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes in horse anti-rabbit IgG (H+L), biotinylated, R.T.U. (Vector: BP-1100). Sections were then washed in 1X TBS-T 3 times. Sections were then incubated in VECTASTAIN Elite ABC reagent, Peroxidase, R.T.U. (PK-7100) for 30 minutes at room temperature. Sections were then washed and then incubated in DAB (Dako: K3467) as per manufacturers protocol. Sections were then rinsed with MilliQ water and washed 3 times in 1X TBS-T for 5 minutes. Sections were then washed in MilliQ water and then counterstained with hematoxylin for 5 minutes. Slides were then washed under running tap water for approximated 15 minutes. Slides were then submerged in 95% and 100% ethanol successively for 2 minutes. Slides were then mounted using toluene and imaged using an Olympus CKX41 microscope. Crypt lengths were measured via the program ImageJ.

TEM
Transmission electron microscopy was performed as previously described (69). Briefly, terminal ileum samples were fixed in Karnovsky’s Fixative (Electron Microscopy Sciences) overnight. The next day, tissues were incubated in 1% osmium tetroxide in 0.1 M PBS pH 7.4 and then dehydrated via a descending ethanol gradient. Dehydrated tissues were then embedded in EMbed 812 resin. 80 nm sections were then cut and placed on formvar coated slot copper grids and counter stained using uranyl acetate and lead citrate. A FEI Tecnai12 BioTwinG2 transmission electron microscope was used to visualized tissues and an AMT XR-60 CCD Digital Camera system was used to acquire images.

Acid-urea polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (AU-PAGE)
Intestinal crypts were isolated as described. Crypts were then resuspended in 30% acetic acid and sonicated. After sonication, lysates were incubated overnight at 4C with agitation. Samples were then diluted threefold and centrifuged with a speed of 100,000 x g at 4C for 2 hours to remove insoluble material. Supernatant was collected and protein concentration was determined via Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kits (23225). Equivalent amounts of protein were then lyophilized. The lyophilized protein was then dissolved in 30 L of AU-PAGE loading buffer (3M urea in 5% (v/v) glacial acetic acid in H O and methyl green). Equivalent amounts of protein was then loaded into AU-PAGE gels and run in 5% acetic acid running buffer with reverse polarity. Gels were run at 150V until proteins reached the bottom. Proteins were then visualized via Coomassie blue staining and densitometry was performed via ImageJ.

Lymphocyte isolation
Lymphocytes were isolated as previously described (70). Briefly, the small intestines were opened, Peyer’s patched and luminal contents were removed, and the tissues were cut into ~2cm pieces. To isolate lamina propria (LP) lymphocytes, the tissues were treated with EDTA (Invitrogen) solution at 37°C with shaking at 220 rpm for 30 min to remove intestinal epithelial cells. The tissues were then digested with Type I collagenase (Gibco) at 37°C with shaking at 300 rpm for 40 min and mashed through 70-μm cell strainers. LP lymphocytes were subsequently isolated using a 44%/67% Percoll gradient.

Flow Cytometry
Intestinal crypts were isolated as described. Crypts were incubated in DMEM/F12 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum for 20 minutes at 4C. Crypts were then disassociated in TrypLE (Invitrogen) with 10μM Rock inhibitor (Y-27632) and 2.5 μg/ml DNAse 1 (Sigma-Aldrich) for 10 minutes at 37C. Single cells were then washed twice in PBS. The following fluorophore-conjugated antibodies were purchased from Invitrogen: anti-CD24 (M1/69), anti-CD45 (30-F11), and anti-Epcam (G8.8). Live/Dead aqua fluorescent reactive dye was purchased from Invitrogen. Cells were then stained with antibodies for 30 minutes at 4C and filtered to remove clumps. Results were acquired with a BD-LSR-Fortessa or cells were sorted using a FACS ARIA IIIU or a CytoFLEX SRT cell sorter.

Lymphocytes were isolated as described. The following fluorophore-conjugated antibodies were purchased from Biolegend, BD Biosciences or eBioscience: anti-CD45 (30-F11), anti-CD3ε (145-2C11), anti-CD19 (6D5), anti-CD11b (Mac-1), anti-Ly6C (HK1.4), anti-Ly6G (1A8), anti-CD64 (S18017D), anti-CD11c (N418), anti-MHC II (M5/114.15.2), anti-NK1.1 (PK136), anti-CD49b (DX5), anti-CD8α (53-6.7), anti-CD103 (2E7), anti-CD127 (A7R34), anti-RORγt (AFKJS-9), anti-Thy1.2 (30-H12), anti-CD4 (RM4-5) and anti-TCRβ (H57-597). Live/Dead dye was purchased from Invitrogen. Cells were incubated with antibodies for 30 min at 4°C in the dark. For transcriptional factor staining, Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer set (Invitrogen) was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were acquired on Aurora (Cytek), and data were analyzed using the FlowJo v.10 software (FlowJo, LLC).

Total RNA Sequencing (RNA-seq)
RNA sequencing and data analysis was performed as previously described (69). Before constructing the Illumina TruSeq Total RNA library, total RNA was quantified using the Qubit RNA BR assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific: Guide MAN0001987 MP10210, Kit #Q10210). RNA quality was assessed on an Agilent 4150 Tapestation (G2992AA) with the Agilent RNA ScreenTape Analysis (Agilent: Publication Part Number: G2991-S90021, Kit #5067-5576). A total of 2.5 μg of RNA was treated with 1 M Baseline-Zero DNase (Epicentre Cat. No DB0711K) according to the Baseline–Zero DNase protocol (www.epicentre.com, Lit # 263). The RNA was then purified and concentrated using 1.8 × volume Agencourt RNAClean XP Beads (Beckman Coulter A63987) following the standard protocol (Protocol 001298v001). RNA concentration was re-measured with the Qubit BR RNA assay kit to prepare for input into the TruSeq Stranded Total RNA library protocol.

Illumina-compatible cDNA libraries with RiboZero Gold depletion were constructed according to the TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Reference Guide (Illumina Document #1000000040499v00, TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Gold Illumina Kit #20020598). Final cDNA library concentrations were determined using the Qubit dsDNA BR assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific: Guide MAN0002325 MP 32850, Kit #Q32850). The quality of the libraries was evaluated by running each on an Agilent 4150 Tapestation using the DNA 1000 Screentape kit (Agilent: Publication Part Number: G2991-90031, Kit #5067-5583). The electropherogram of each library was analyzed using Agilent 4150 Tapestation Analysis Software (Version 3.1) with a range of 200–600 bp to determine the average library size. Average size and concentration were used to calculate the molarity of each library. Libraries were pooled and denatured according to the Illumina Denature and Dilute Libraries Guide for the NextSeq System (Illumina Part #15048776). The denatured libraries were loaded onto an Illumina NextSeq 550 v2.5 Mid 150 output reagent cartridge (Illumina #20024904) at a final concentration of 1.5 pM in HT1 buffer, with 1% PhiX control library v3 (Illumina #FC-110-3001) added. Paired-end 75 bp single-index sequencing was performed, generating approximately 7.5 million paired-end reads per sample.

Sequencing analysis was carried out using RNA-seq for Eukaryotes Analysis v3 by the Banana Slug Genomics Center at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Raw paired-end sequencing reads from the Illumina sequencer were assessed for potential issues and contaminants using FastQC. Adapter sequences and primers were removed from the reads using Trimmomatic, followed by trimming of polyA tails, polyN sequences, and any reads with quality scores below 28 using PRINSEQ. Any reads shorter than 20 bp after trimming were discarded. A second round of quality control with FastQC was performed to compare read quality before and after trimming. The trimmed reads were mapped to the reference genome (GRCm38/mm10) using TopHat2, with NCBI RefSeq annotated genes as the transcriptome index. Read alignment coverage and summary statistics were computed using SAMtools, BEDtools, and UCSC Genome Browser utilities. For abundance estimation and differential expression analysis, the Cufflinks 2.2.0 workflow and read-counting methods using DESeq and edgeR were employed. Specifically, the sequencing reads aligned to RefSeq annotated genes were quantified using Cuffquant, and gene expression levels across the samples were normalized using Cuffnorm with FPKM values computed for sample correlation assessment. Differential expression analysis was performed using Cuffdiff on the results from Cuffquant. Additionally, HTSeq was used to compute raw read counts for the annotated RefSeq genes. Raw read counts were normalized across all samples and used for differential expression analysis with edgeR.

16S Microbial Sequencing
Mouse cecal samples were collected and stored at -80C. Cecal samples were shipped on ice. Fecal DNA was extracted via Qiagen DNeasy PowerLyser PowerSoil Kit (Qiagen). Bead beating step was performed following the manufacturer’s instructions (PowerLyzer 24 Homogenizer, Omni International). The 16S microbial sequencing was performed as previously described (71).

AD-Adam17 and Ad-Y5 Infection
HEK293 cells were infected with 100 MOI of with either Ad-Adam17 or Ad-Y5 overnight and were harvested for RT-PCR to confirm upregulation. Ad-Adam17 and Ad-Y5 were generated as previously described (72). Mice were injected intraperitoneally with either Ad-Adam17 or Ad-Y5 at a concentration of 1x10^9 pfu/mouse. Mice were then irradiated 6 days post injection and processed as described above.

ADAM17 Activity Assay
ADAM17 Fluorogenic Kit (BPS Bioscience) was utilized for ADAM17 activity assays as per manufacture’s protocol. Briefly, ADAM17 protein was incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes with or without 4mM H O . ADAM17 fluorogenic substrate was then added and results were collected every 10 minutes for 250 minutes utilizing a HTS 7000 Bio Assay Reader.

Statistical Analysis
Bacterial dissemination, RT-qPCR, ELISA and all counting experiments were analyzed via non-parametric Mann-Whitney test, two tailed or Welch’s t-test using GraphPad/Prizim. Paired samples were analyzed via Wilcox test using GraphPad/Prizim. Grouped experiments were performed via two way ANOVA. Outliers were determined by using GraphPad Prism (ROUT analysis, Q=1%). More specific statistical analysis details can be found in the figure legend of each figure. Cell counts were performed from at least 30 crypts per mouse.
Microbiome analysis was performed in R (version 4.3.1). Data was formatted utilizing phyloseq (version 1.44.0). Specifically, to normalize data we filtered taxa with a relative abundance of  1e-4, Total Sum Scaled (TSS) abundances to 1e6, and performed a general log transformation. We calculated the beta diversity metric, Weighted UniFrac, and identified significance, using ADONIS, with the vegan package (version 2.6.6.1). To calculate LEfSe we utilized the microbiomeMarker (version 1.6.0) package. All plots were created with ggplot2 (version 3.5.1).

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this study, Kempen et al. reported that IL-17A-IL-17RA signalling in Paneth cells is critical for host defence responses in the small intestine. The authors also revealed that IL-17A-induced Nox1 is necessary for the subsequent tissue regeneration responses mediated by ADAM17 enzymatic activity. To provide in vivo evidence to support their conclusions, the authors used a series of Paneth cell-specific knockout mice, including Il17rafl/fl Defa6-cre and Adam17fl/fl Defa6-cre. This study is likely to attract wide attention from scientists involved in mucosal immunology.
Overall, the observations and underlying implications described here are both reasonable and significant. The experiments are rigorous, with sufficient replicates and controls. However, it is well known that intestinal epithelial cells are a major IL-17A-targeting cell type in the gut, and that IL-17A is considered a protective cytokine at the mucosal surface because it can induce antibacterial peptides and work synergistically with IL-22. Therefore, these previous reports and existing knowledge compromise the novelty of the current study.
My only major concern about this study is that the authors only used Il17rafl/fl Defa6-cre mice to represent a genetic deficiency in IL-17A signalling in Paneth cells. However, IL-17RA is the receptor for all IL-17 family cytokines. IL-17RC deficiency is more relevant to claiming the specific effects of IL-17A/F. IL-17RA deficiency cannot rule out the effects mediated by IL-17C, since IL-17RA forms a heterodimer with IL-17RE in response to IL-17C, and IL-17C-IL-17RA/RE signalling has also been reported to play an important role in maintaining mucosal homeostasis. Therefore, the authors should rule out or include the effects of IL-17C in their study.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript “Immune cell-derived IL-17A promotes Paneth cell dedifferentiation through the Nox1-ADAM17 axis to regenerate the gut epithelium” by Kempen et al. describes a novel function of IL-17RA signaling in regulating the reprogramming of Paneth cells into multipotent stem-like cells upon irradiation. By selectively knocking out IL-17RA in Defa6-expressing Paneth cells, the authors provide evidence that Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA signaling protects against irradiation-induced intestinal damage.
Using Paneth cell lineage-tracing mice, they further show that Paneth cells can acquire stem cell–like features following intestinal injury, a process that can be blocked by neutralizing IL-17A with antibodies. Mechanistically, the study demonstrates that IL-17A increases ADAM17 expression in Paneth cells. Notably, Paneth cell–specific ADAM17 knockout phenocopied the IL-17RA knockout in the context of irradiation-induced injury, while ectopic ADAM17 expression rescued the effects of IL-17RA deficiency.
The manuscript also establishes a link between IL-17RA–dependent Nox1 expression, ROS production, and ROS-mediated ADAM17 activation. Pharmacological inhibition of ROS with NAC suppressed the dedifferentiation of Paneth cells into stem-like cells after irradiation, suggesting a central role for ROS in injury-induced Paneth cell plasticity. Finally, the authors indicate that ADAM17 promotes tissue regeneration primarily by enhancing cellular proliferation rather than by modulating gut barrier proteins.
The findings are highly exciting and of significant scientific interest, as they identify a novel function of IL-17RA signaling in regulating Paneth cell reprogramming during intestinal injury. It has become increasingly clear that Paneth cells play a central role in maintaining intestinal integrity—not only through their functions as innate immune cells and as stem cell niche supporters but also by serving as an alternative stem cell population that contributes to intestinal regeneration following tissue damage. While defects in Paneth cell function have long been associated with the development of intestinal inflammatory diseases, recent evidence shows that the reacquisition of stem cell features during inflammation can also enable Paneth cells to give rise to intestinal tumors (Verhagen et al., 2024 DOI: 10.1038/s41588-024-01801-y). In light of these diverse roles of Paneth cells in both health and disease, it is critical to better understand how their fate is extrinsically regulated.
Kempen et al. have invested considerable effort in studying the role of IL-17RA signaling in Paneth cells by employing several transgenic mouse lines and ex vivo organoid systems, providing strong support for a role of IL-17A signaling in regulating Paneth cell plasticity. Their findings may also have translational relevance, as they could open new avenues for the treatment of IBD or for supportive care during irradiation therapy. In this regard, the authors should consider performing additional experiments to broaden the translational impact of their study.
As IL-17RA signaling appears to be dispensable for Paneth cell dedifferentiation during DSS-induced gastroenteritis (Lin et al., 2022 DOI: 10.1016/j.immuni.2021.12.016), the mechanism described by Kempen et al. does not seem to be universal, but rather context-dependent and influenced by the type of injury. It would therefore be valuable to examine whether Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA signaling is also relevant for intestinal regeneration following chemotherapy, thereby expanding the potential scope of IL-17A–based supportive care.
Moreover, it would strengthen the study to assess whether a similar mechanism might apply to colonic regeneration. Recent findings indicate that Paneth-like Deep Crypt Secretory (DCS) cells in the colon can revert to stem-like cells to support tissue repair during colitis (Xu et al., 2025 DOI: 10.1038/s41418-025-01471-1). The authors could, for example, evaluate whether DCS proliferation is impaired in irradiated IEC-specific IL-17RA knockout mice (e.g. by co-staining PCNA or Ki67 with DCS markers such as Reg4, c-Kit, or WGA), or at least determine whether colonic damage is exacerbated upon epithelial loss of IL-17RA or blockade of IL-17A signaling with neutralizing antibodies. Demonstrating that IL-17RA signaling also contributes to colonic regeneration would substantially enhance the relevance of the study with relatively limited additional effort.
Beyond these points, I have additional critical remarks and questions that should be addressed prior to considering this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications. These points are summarized in bullet-point format for clarity:
1. First, and perhaps the most crucial experiment missing to convincingly demonstrate that IL-17RA directly regulates Paneth cell dedifferentiation, is the analysis of lineage tracing in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre;mTmG mice. I am somewhat surprised that the authors did not do this experiment. Although the anti-IL17A antibody treatment causes a reduction of Defa6-lineage tracing it might be due to other indirect mechanisms.
2. Likewise, irradiation-induced Paneth cell lineage tracing should be assessed in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre;mTmG mice. Alternatively, Paneth cell proliferation should be quantified by co-staining proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67 or PCNA) with Paneth cell–specific markers such as lysozyme to support the importance of ADAM17 for Paneth cell dedifferentiation.
3. As the authors introduce the depletion and re-appearance of canonical ISCs upon irradiation (Fig. 2B), they should address whether the regeneration of canonical ISCs is impaired in IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice (e.g. by a simple OLFM4 staining or Lgr5 in situ hybridization).
4. Kempen and colleagues claim increased intestinal damage in IL17RA whole-body knockout mice or in mice with IL17RA knockout in IECs. Although they demonstrate increased bacterial dissemination in the spleen and liver, the only reported evidence of enhanced tissue damage is a minor reduction in crypt length. Why did the authors not include additional parameters such as villus length, weight loss, quantification of viable crypts (as in Metcalfe et al., 2014 PMID: 24332836), or quantification of PCNA+ cells, as they performed in Fig. 3D for the Paneth cell–specific knockout? The same concern applies to the mice treated with IL17A antibodies (Figure 5) and the mice overexpressing ADAM17 (Figure 6). The inclusion of some additional parameters would provide stronger support for their claim.
5. In Figure 2C, the authors report reduced Lyz mRNA levels in the intestinal epithelium of IL17RA knockout mice after irradiation, which led them to further investigate IL17RA signaling in Paneth cells. However, it remains unclear whether this reduction is due to decreased lysozyme expression within Paneth cells or to a reduction in Paneth cell numbers upon loss of IL17RA. To address this, Paneth cells should be stained and quantified. Similarly, Paneth cell numbers and lysozyme expression should be evaluated in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice and IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, in order to determine whether a decrease in lysozyme expression can be also observed upon tissue or Paneth cell specific Il17RA knockout.
6. Regarding the effects on lysozyme expression upon IL17RA knockout, I have another critical remark: in their prior study (Lin et al., 2022 PMID: 35081371), the authors reported no difference of lysozyme expression in the intestinal epithelium of 6-week-old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice, while Paneth cell number was reduced in 10-week-old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice. In the current manuscript, the only information provided about mouse age is found in the Methods section, where it is stated that animals were between 6 and 15 weeks old. Given the previously described age-dependent effects of IL17RA deletion on Paneth cells, it is essential to indicate the exact age of the mice used in each experiment.
7. In Figure 4, the authors dedicate an entire section to different Paneth cell populations, mentioning a Defa6-low population, expressing stem cell genes. These cells likely represent Paneth cell progenitors, potentially more prone to dedifferentiate than Defa6-high/OLFM4-low cells. However, no experiments were performed to address this. For example, this could have been tested by analysing the organoid-forming capacity sorted Defa6-YFP high and low or Defa6-GFP high/CD24+ and Defa6-GFP low/CD24+ cells following irradiation. At minimum, the authors should discuss the possibility that the differentiation status of Paneth cells may influence their ability to dedifferentiate upon injury.
8. The authors show lineage tracing in Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice upon irradiation (Figure 5A) as well as organoid growth from sorted GFP+CD24+ cells from these mice (Figure 5B). However, no quantification is provided for the lineage tracing frequency (i.e. the number of tracings per GFP labelled crypt) between non-irradiated and irradiated mice, nor is there quantification of the number of GFP+ organoids per plated cells to indicate the efficiency of Paneth cells to dedifferentiate. In Figure 5D and Figure 6K, the authors do quantify single GFP+ cells and GFP+ clones in crypts and villi, but it is not explained how these quantifications were performed or what the y-axis represents. This information should be clarified.
9. In Figure 5G, the authors claim to provide evidence for increased Paneth cell lineage tracing in IL17A-treated organoids. I find this interpretation unconvincing: the images do not show ribbons of GFP+ cells that would indicate lineage tracing but rather single GFP+ cells distributed in organoid buddings, consistent with the normal localization of Paneth cells. A more likely explanation is that IL17A treatment enhances Paneth cell differentiation, similar to what they reported previously (Lin et al., 2022 PMID: 35081371). The authors might argue that organoid passaging results in fully GFP-labelled organoids; however, the images in Figures 5H and 5I are also not convincing in this regard. Instead, they appear more consistent with immature spheres, though this is difficult to assess because no bright-field images were provided to illustrate organoid morphology. Stronger evidence is needed to convincingly demonstrate Paneth cell dedifferentiation ex vivo.
10. The rationale behind the selection of genes analyzed in the context of Paneth cell dedifferentiation (Figure 6A) is not entirely clear. For example, why did the authors examine Wnt9b and Wnt6 to assess Wnt signaling rather than canonical Wnt target genes such as Axin2, CyclinD1, c-Myc, or CD44? Similarly, why were Dll1 and Dll4 measured instead of established Notch target genes such as HES or HEY to evaluate pathway activity? In addition, the authors did not include YAP target genes, despite their own re-analysis of scRNA-seq data showing that YAP targets are upregulated in the same Paneth cell subcluster with the highest expression of ADAM17 and Nox1 (Figure 6H). Likewise, in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, the authors measured expression of Hif1α, Hk2, Slc2a1, and Pgk1, but only Hif1α is discussed in the text. What was the rationale for including the other genes?
11. The title of the manuscript suggests that Paneth cell dedifferentiation is regulated through the NOX1–ADAM17 axis, which is a strong claim given that the only evidence indicating an involvement of NOX1 is the upregulation of NOX1 mRNA upon irradiation and IL-17A treatment, and the downregulation of NOX1 mRNA in irradiated ADAM17fl/fl; Defa6-Cre mice. At a minimum, effects on NOX1 expression should be confirmed at the protein level, ideally by immunostaining in mouse tissues. Additionally, demonstrating reduced ROS production upon Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA knockout (e.g., by ROS analysis in irradiated organoids using indicators such as CellROX or H2DCFDA) would further strengthen the proposed link between IL-17RA signaling and ROS-mediated ADAM17 activation. Even then, the title might falsely indicate regulation by NOX1, as ROS might be increased by multiple other mechanisms upon irradiation.
12. Regarding the title, I have an additional remark: the authors do not provide direct evidence that the observed effect is specifically mediated by immune cell–derived IL-17A. To be accurate, either immune cells should be removed from the title, or experiments should be included to specifically address their involvement. Notably, IL-17A can be expressed by other cell types, such as fibroblasts, as reported by Lotti et al., 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20131195).
13. As stated in the main text, ADAM17 is expressed in Paneth cells of both naïve and irradiated mice (Fig. S5A). Based on the images, ADAM17 expression appears to be considerably lower in irradiated mice compared to non-irradiated controls. The authors neither comment on this nor provide further analysis of differential ADAM17 expression between the two conditions. If confirmed, this would contradict the results shown in Figure 6H, where re-analysis of published scRNA-seq data from irradiated mice indicated increased ADAM17 expression. This discrepancy should be addressed and discussed.
14. Figure S6 is intended to show a Paneth cell–specific ADAM17 knockout; however, ADAM17 expression also appears reduced in other epithelial cells. Here either higher-quality images should be provided to clarify this or it should be commented on why a Paneth cell–specific knockout might lead to a broader reduction of ADAM17 expression.
15. Figure 6K shows a reduction of lineage tracing in NAC-treated mice. Is it possible to assess ADAM17 activity in these mice? This would help to strengthen the link between ROS production and ADAM17 activation.
16. Regarding Figure 7F, Kempen et al. state that there is no difference in the tight junction protein ZO-1 in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre mice and conclude that ADAM17 limits damage in response to irradiation by promoting cellular proliferation rather than modulating gut barrier proteins. However, based on the images provided in Figure 7F, it appears that ZO-1 is absent in the crypts of Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre mice. The authors should either reconsider their statement or provide additional data to support their interpretation.
In addition to the above I have some minor remarks:
1. In Figure 1A and F, Figure 3A, Figure 5E, Figure 6M, Figure 7A, Figure S3A it is not described what the arrows should indicate.
2. Y-axes in Figure 1A,, 3A, 5E, 6M, 7A, 7D should start from 0.
3. It is not described how PCNA+ cells in Figure 3D and Figure 7D were quantified (cells per crypt? How many crypts per mouse?)
4. Authors should describe in more detail how outliers were identified and in which experiments outliers were excluded.
5. It is not always clear how many times the experiments were repeated or how many samples were analyzed and quantified. For example, the authors state: “Figures 5A, 5B, 5G, and 5I are representative of 2–3 mice. Figures 5B, 5D, 5E, 5G, and 5H are generated from 2–3 independent experiments, and representative images are shown and quantified.” This level of reporting is insufficient for a high-quality journal such as Nature Communications. The exact number of biological and technical replicates, as well as the precise number of mice analyzed in each experiment, must be clearly specified.
6. The manuscript refers to Figure S6A, however, Figure S6 has no A or B.
Altogether, in my opinion considerable additional work is required for the manuscript to reach the high standard expected for Nature Communications. Nonetheless, I am confident that the authors can address the points raised, and that, with these revisions the manuscript could make a significant impact in the field.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

Dear Reviewers,
We would like to thank the reviewers for their consideration of our manuscript and for
providing insightful comments. In addition, we appreciate the opportunity to revise and
resubmit this manuscript. We found reviewer comments to be helpful and note that the
reviewers provided many enthusiastic comments. Based on their suggestions, we have
added new data that supports our findings. Specifically, we demonstrate that: 1) IL-17C
does not promote fully green organoid development after irradiation or Paneth cell lineage
tracer organoids, 2) Paneth cell specific proliferation is reduced in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre+
mice, 3) there is reduced cellular proliferation in IL-17RA KO, Il17RAfl/fl;villin-cre+,
and anti-IL-17A administered lineage tracer mice. Furthermore, cellular proliferation is
increased when Adam17 expression is increased, 4) fully green organoids derived from
irradiated and IL-17A treated Paneth cell lineage tracer organoid contain terminally
differentiated epithelial cells and 5) NOX1 protein is reduced in the ileum of both
Il17RAfl/fl;Defa6-Cre+, and ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre+ mice. Also, we made modifications to
the text, which are highlighted in yellow. Overall, the reviewers’ comments and
suggestions helped us significantly strengthen our manuscript. Below, we provide each
of the reviewers’ comments followed by a detailed point-by-point response.
Reviewer 1:
Summary and Significance: In this study, Kempen et al. reported that IL-17A-IL-17RA
signalling in Paneth cells is critical for host defence responses in the small intestine.
The authors also revealed that IL-17A-induced Nox1 is necessary for the subsequent
tissue regeneration responses mediated by ADAM17 enzymatic activity. To provide in
vivo evidence to support their conclusions, the authors used a series of Paneth cell-
specific knockout mice, including Il17rafl/fl Defa6-cre and Adam17fl/fl Defa6-cre. This
study is likely to attract wide attention from scientists involved in mucosal immunology.
Overall, the observations and underlying implications described here are both
reasonable and significant. The experiments are rigorous, with sufficient replicates and
controls. However, it is well known that intestinal epithelial cells are a major IL-17A-
targeting cell type in the gut, and that IL-17A is considered a protective cytokine at the
mucosal surface because it can induce antibacterial peptides and work synergistically
with IL-22. Therefore, these previous reports and existing knowledge compromise the
novelty of the current study.
Comment: My only major concern about this study is that the authors only used
Il17rafl/fl Defa6-cre mice to represent a genetic deficiency in IL-17A signalling in Paneth
cells. However, IL-17RA is the receptor for all IL-17 family cytokines. IL-17RC deficiency
is more relevant to claiming the specific effects of IL-17A/F. IL-17RA deficiency cannot
rule out the effects mediated by IL-17C, since IL-17RA forms a heterodimer with IL-
17RE in response to IL-17C, and IL-17C-IL-17RA/RE signalling has also been reported
to play an important role in maintaining mucosal homeostasis. Therefore, the authors
should rule out or include the effects of IL-17C in their study.
Response I thank the reviewer for the recommendation to consider the effects of IL-
17C in this study. Following the approach used for IL-25 (Fig. S3C), we tested whether
recombinant IL-17C stimulation in irradiated Paneth cell-specific lineage-tracer mice
could induce green organoid development after irradiation. We did not observe a
significant increase in green organoid formation following IL-17C treatment (Fig. S3C).
In addition, we have revised the manuscript title to emphasize that IL-17RA signaling in
Paneth cells promotes acquisition of stem-like properties, rather than attributing this
effect specifically to IL-17A.
Reviewer 2:
Summary and Significance: The manuscript “Immune cell-derived IL-17A promotes
Paneth cell dedifferentiation through the Nox1-ADAM17 axis to regenerate the gut
epithelium” by Kempen et al. describes a novel function of IL-17RA signaling in
regulating the reprogramming of Paneth cells into multipotent stem-like cells upon
irradiation. By selectively knocking out IL-17RA in Defa6-expressing Paneth cells, the
authors provide evidence that Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA signaling protects against
irradiation-induced intestinal damage.
Using Paneth cell lineage-tracing mice, they further show that Paneth cells can acquire
stem cell–like features following intestinal injury, a process that can be blocked by
neutralizing IL-17A with antibodies. Mechanistically, the study demonstrates that IL-17A
increases ADAM17 expression in Paneth cells. Notably, Paneth cell–specific ADAM17
knockout phenocopied the IL-17RA knockout in the context of irradiation-induced injury,
while ectopic ADAM17 expression rescued the effects of IL-17RA deficiency.
The manuscript also establishes a link between IL-17RA–dependent Nox1 expression,
ROS production, and ROS-mediated ADAM17 activation. Pharmacological inhibition of
ROS with NAC suppressed the dedifferentiation of Paneth cells into stem-like cells after
irradiation, suggesting a central role for ROS in injury-induced Paneth cell plasticity.
Finally, the authors indicate that ADAM17 promotes tissue regeneration primarily by
enhancing cellular proliferation rather than by modulating gut barrier proteins.
The findings are highly exciting and of significant scientific interest, as they identify a
novel function of IL-17RA signaling in regulating Paneth cell reprogramming during
intestinal injury. It has become increasingly clear that Paneth cells play a central role in
maintaining intestinal integrity—not only through their functions as innate immune cells
and as stem cell niche supporters but also by serving as an alternative stem cell
population that contributes to intestinal regeneration following tissue damage. While
defects in Paneth cell function have long been associated with the development of
intestinal inflammatory diseases, recent evidence shows that the reacquisition of stem
cell features during inflammation can also enable Paneth cells to give rise to intestinal
tumors (Verhagen et al., 2024 DOI: 10.1038/s41588-024-01801-y). In light of these
diverse roles of Paneth cells in both health and disease, it is critical to better understand
how their fate is extrinsically regulated.
Kempen et al. have invested considerable effort in studying the role of IL-17RA
signaling in Paneth cells by employing several transgenic mouse lines and ex vivo
organoid systems, providing strong support for a role of IL-17A signaling in regulating
Paneth cell plasticity. Their findings may also have translational relevance, as they
could open new avenues for the treatment of IBD or for supportive care during
irradiation therapy. In this regard, the authors should consider performing additional
experiments to broaden the translational impact of their study.
Major Comments
Comment: As IL-17RA signaling appears to be dispensable for Paneth cell
dedifferentiation during DSS-induced gastroenteritis (Lin et al., 2022 DOI:
10.1016/j.immuni.2021.12.016), the mechanism described by Kempen et al. does not
seem to be universal, but rather context-dependent and influenced by the type of injury.
It would therefore be valuable to examine whether Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA
signaling is also relevant for intestinal regeneration following chemotherapy, thereby
expanding the potential scope of IL-17A–based supportive care. Moreover, it would
strengthen the study to assess whether a similar mechanism might apply to colonic
regeneration. Recent findings indicate that Paneth-like Deep Crypt Secretory (DCS)
cells in the colon can revert to stem-like cells to support tissue repair during colitis (Xu
et al., 2025 DOI: 10.1038/s41418-025-01471-1). The authors could, for example,
evaluate whether DCS proliferation is impaired in irradiated IEC-specific IL-17RA
knockout mice (e.g. by co-staining PCNA or Ki67 with DCS markers such as Reg4, c-
Kit, or WGA), or at least determine whether colonic damage is exacerbated upon
epithelial loss of IL-17RA or blockade of IL-17A signaling with neutralizing antibodies.
Demonstrating that IL-17RA signaling also contributes to colonic regeneration would
substantially enhance the relevance of the study with relatively limited additional effort.
Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer 2 for their thoughtful comment and valuable
insight. We agree that investigating whether IL-17RA signaling in Paneth-like Deep
Crypt Secretory (DCS) cells of the colon may promote reversion to a stem-like state and
contribute to tissue repair during colitis is a compelling and important question.
However, we believe this direction falls outside the scope of the current study. Our work
is specifically focused on the small intestine and bona fide Paneth cells, whose plasticity
and contribution to epithelial regeneration have been well characterized in prior
literature. Our experimental approach, conditional knockout mice, Paneth cells lineage
tracer mice, resources, and analyses were therefore designed to address this defined
biological context. We fully agree that examining IL-17RA signaling in colonic DCS cells
represents an intriguing and valuable avenue for future research, and it may serve as
the basis for a separate, dedicated study in the future. We are grateful to the reviewer
for highlighting this possibility.
Comment: First, and perhaps the most crucial experiment missing to convincingly
demonstrate that IL-17RA directly regulates Paneth cell dedifferentiation, is the analysis
of lineage tracing in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre;mTmG mice. I am somewhat
surprised that the authors did not do this experiment. Although the anti-IL17A antibody
treatment causes a reduction of Defa6-lineage tracing it might be due to other indirect
mechanisms.
Response: We agree with reviewer 2. Utilizing Il17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre;mTmG mice to
demonstrate that IL-17RA directly regulates Paneth cell dedifferentiation would have
been a very strong piece of data to support our story. We discussed trying to do this,
unfortunately developing this mice line would be very challenging. Please refer to the
following reply from The Jackson Laboratory in response to our inquiry of developing
these mice:
“The Il17ra and ROSA26 (insertion site of the mT/mG transgene) are tightly linked on
mouse chromosome 6. They are only ~7 Mbp apart. If you are going to need to
generate mice that are homozygous for the Il17ra<tm2.1Koll> loxp-flanked allele AND
carrying the Gt(ROSA)26Sor,tm4(ACTB-tdTomato,-EGFP)Luo. Transgene (as a
heterozygote or a homozygote), you will need a meiotic recombination event to put both
the Il17ra<tm2.1Koll> and the Gt(ROSA)26Sor,tm4(ACTB-tdTomato,-EGFP)Luo alleles
on the same copy of mouse chromosome 6. As the two loci are so close together, the
chances of that are low. It may be very difficult (as in needing to generate a lot of mice),
or not possible.”
Thus, we decided to utilize anti-IL17A treatment and recombinant IL-17A with our
Paneth cell lineage tracing mice as an alternative approach.
Comment: Likewise, irradiation-induced Paneth cell lineage tracing should be assessed
in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre;mTmG mice. Alternatively, Paneth cell proliferation should be
quantified by co-staining proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67 or PCNA) with Paneth cell–
specific markers such as lysozyme to support the importance of ADAM17 for Paneth
cell dedifferentiation.
Response: We stained and quantified Paneth cell specific proliferation in
Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre mice via co-staining PCNA and Lyz1 as recommended by the
reviewer. We observed significant reduction of Lyz1+/PCNA+ double positive cells in
cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice (Fig. 7E).
Comment: As the authors introduce the depletion and re-appearance of canonical ISCs
upon irradiation (Fig. 2B), they should address whether the regeneration of canonical
ISCs is impaired in IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice (e.g. by a simple OLFM4 staining or Lgr5
in situ hybridization).
Response: We stained for OLFM4 in both naïve and irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/-
mice. As expected, we saw reduced amounts of Olfm4+ crypts in mice 5 days post
irradiation as compared to non-irradiated mice. Interestingly, we also observed
decreased amounts of Olfm4+ crypts in irradiated Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as
compared to irradiated cre- mice. This revealed that canonical ISCs regeneration was
indeed impaired in Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice as compared to cre- mice 5 days post
irradiation (Fig. 3E).
Comment: Kempen and colleagues claim increased intestinal damage in IL17RA
whole-body knockout mice or in mice with IL17RA knockout in IECs. Although they
demonstrate increased bacterial dissemination in the spleen and liver, the only reported
evidence of enhanced tissue damage is a minor reduction in crypt length. Why did the
authors not include additional parameters such as villus length, weight loss,
quantification of viable crypts (as in Metcalfe et al., 2014 PMID: 24332836), or
quantification of PCNA+ cells, as they performed in Fig. 3D for the Paneth cell–specific
knockout? The same concern applies to the mice treated with IL17A antibodies (Figure
5) and the mice overexpressing ADAM17 (Figure 6). The inclusion of some additional
parameters would provide stronger support for their claim.
Response: Our initial measurements were of the crypt/villus structure. Specifically, we
measure from the base of the crypt to the top of the villi. We have clarified this in our
main text. Furthermore, we stained and quantified PCNA+ cells all of our other
experiments, as suggested. We observed reduced cellular proliferation in Il17ra-/-, villin-
cre+, and anti-IL-17A treated lineage tracer mice. Furthermore, cellular proliferation is
increased when Adam17 expression is increased (Figs. 1D, 1J, 5F, & 6N). Lastly, we
did not record weight loss in any experiments as the mice are irradiated and thus bone
marrow ablated and immunodeficient. Thus, handling them may lead to contamination,
which we wanted to minimize.
Comment: In Figure 2C, the authors report reduced Lyz mRNA levels in the intestinal
epithelium of IL17RA knockout mice after irradiation, which led them to further
investigate IL17RA signaling in Paneth cells. However, it remains unclear whether this
reduction is due to decreased lysozyme expression within Paneth cells or to a reduction
in Paneth cell numbers upon loss of IL17RA. To address this, Paneth cells should be
stained and quantified. Similarly, Paneth cell numbers and lysozyme expression should
be evaluated in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice and IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, in
order to determine whether a decrease in lysozyme expression can be also observed
upon tissue or Paneth cell specific Il17RA knockout.
Response: As recommended, we stained for Lyz1 in tissue from irradiated Il17ra KO,
Il17rafl/fl;villin-cre+/-, and Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice. We observed decreased Lyz1+
cells in the ileum of Il17ra KO and Il17rafl/fl;villin-cre+ mice as compared to their WT and
cre- counterparts (Figs. 2D & E). There was no difference in Lyz1+ cells in the ileum
between and Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice (Fig. S1J).
Comment: Regarding the effects on lysozyme expression upon IL17RA knockout, I
have another critical remark: in their prior study (Lin et al., 2022 PMID: 35081371), the
authors reported no difference of lysozyme expression in the intestinal epithelium of 6-
week-old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice, while Paneth cell number was reduced in 10-week-
old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice. In the current manuscript, the only information provided
about mouse age is found in the Methods section, where it is stated that animals were
between 6 and 15 weeks old. Given the previously described age-dependent effects of
IL17RA deletion on Paneth cells, it is essential to indicate the exact age of the mice
used in each experiment.
Response: We have added the mice ages of all mice used in the figure legends.
Comment: In Figure 4, the authors dedicate an entire section to different Paneth cell
populations, mentioning a Defa6-low population, expressing stem cell genes. These
cells likely represent Paneth cell progenitors, potentially more prone to dedifferentiate
than Defa6-high/OLFM4-low cells. However, no experiments were performed to address
this. For example, this could have been tested by analysing the organoid-forming
capacity sorted Defa6-YFP high and low or Defa6-GFP high/CD24+ and Defa6-GFP
low/CD24+ cells following irradiation. At minimum, the authors should discuss the
possibility that the differentiation status of Paneth cells may influence their ability to
dedifferentiate upon injury.
Response: We have discussed the possibility that the differentiation status of Paneth
cells may influence their ability to dedifferentiate upon injury. We have added this in the
discussion section (lines 439-442). Specifically, we state: “We believe these Paneth
progenitor cells drive Paneth cell specific regeneration post irradiation injury rather than mature
Paneth cells. Paneth progenitor cells have a unique expression profile (high Il17ra/rc and
Olfm4) which allows them to be primed for rapid dedifferentiation in response to injury and
increased IL-17A signaling.” Furthermore, we have changed our title to explicitly state that we
believe Paneth progenitors drive regeneration in our study.
Comment: The authors show lineage tracing in Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice upon
irradiation (Figure 5A) as well as organoid growth from sorted GFP+CD24+ cells from
these mice (Figure 5B). However, no quantification is provided for the lineage tracing
frequency (i.e. the number of tracings per GFP labelled crypt) between non-irradiated
and irradiated mice, nor is there quantification of the number of GFP+ organoids per
plated cells to indicate the efficiency of Paneth cells to dedifferentiate. In Figure 5D and
Figure 6K, the authors do quantify single GFP+ cells and GFP+ clones in crypts and
villi, but it is not explained how these quantifications were performed or what the y-axis
represents. This information should be clarified.
Response: We have quantified lineage tracing in Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice upon
irradiation (Fig. 5A). Furthermore, we have explained how we quantified figures 5D and
6K in the text. Specifically, we state: “We then counted the number of GFP+ cells in the
base of the crypt and in the villi between the two treatment groups 5 days post
irradiation. We also counted the number of GFP+ clones, which we define as at least 4
GFP+ cells in a row, in the villi between the two treatment groups 5 days post
irradiation.” We also updated the y-axis titles so they are more easily understood.
Comment: In Figure 5G, the authors claim to provide evidence for increased Paneth
cell lineage tracing in IL17A-treated organoids. I find this interpretation unconvincing:
the images do not show ribbons of GFP+ cells that would indicate lineage tracing but
rather single GFP+ cells distributed in organoid buddings, consistent with the normal
localization of Paneth cells. A more likely explanation is that IL17A treatment enhances
Paneth cell differentiation, similar to what they reported previously (Lin et al., 2022
PMID: 35081371). The authors might argue that organoid passaging results in fully
GFP-labelled organoids; however, the images in Figures 5H and 5I are also not
convincing in this regard. Instead, they appear more consistent with immature spheres,
though this is difficult to assess because no bright-field images were provided to
illustrate organoid morphology. Stronger evidence is needed to convincingly
demonstrate Paneth cell dedifferentiation ex vivo.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important point. Our data show that IL-17A
not only increases Paneth cell numbers but also enhances their stem-like properties.
Because the organoids begin to die after five days in culture, we trypsinize them at that
stage to study stem-like Paneth cells. As suggested, we have performed additional
experiments to further support a role for IL-17A in Paneth cell dedifferentiation.We have
provided cleared images and brightfield images in figure 5I which illustrate mature
organoid morphology (Fig. 5I). Lastly, we then stained the IL-17A treated green
organoids for MUC2 and ChGA. MUC2 marks terminally differentiated goblet cells while
ChGA marks terminally differentiated enteroendocrine cells. Since the staining revealed
that these green organoids were composed of both GFP+/MUC2+ double positive cells
and GFP+/ChGA+ double positive cells, we can ascertain that these green organoids
arise from Paneth cells and are mature organoids composed of terminally differentiated
epithelial cells (Fig. 5J).
Comment: The rationale behind the selection of genes analyzed in the context of
Paneth cell dedifferentiation (Figure 6A) is not entirely clear. For example, why did the
authors examine Wnt9b and Wnt6 to assess Wnt signaling rather than canonical Wnt
target genes such as Axin2, CyclinD1, c-Myc, or CD44? Similarly, why were Dll1 and
Dll4 measured instead of established Notch target genes such as HES or HEY to
evaluate pathway activity? In addition, the authors did not include YAP target genes,
despite their own re-analysis of scRNA-seq data showing that YAP targets are
upregulated in the same Paneth cell subcluster with the highest expression of ADAM17
and Nox1 (Figure 6H). Likewise, in irradiated IL17RAfl/fl;Defa6-cre mice, the authors
measured expression of Hif1α, Hk2, Slc2a1, and Pgk1, but only Hif1α is discussed in
the text. What was the rationale for including the other genes?
Response: We have included analysis of canonical Wnt target genes (Axin2, CyclinD1,
c-Myc, and Cd44). We have also included established Notch target gene (Hes1).
In addition, we included YAP target genes (Yap and Hbegf). We did not observe a
difference between the expression of these genes in the ileum between irradiated
Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/- mice (Fig. S4A). We have altered the text to include the rationale
of including Hk2, Slc2a1, and Pgk1 (line 341). Specifically, we state: “Hif1 has been
shown to promote Adam17 expression (46, 47). Thus, we explored if the expression of Hif1
and its target genes (Hk2, Slc2a1, Pgk1) were also reduced in in the terminal ileum of irradiated
Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+ mice.”
Comment: The title of the manuscript suggests that Paneth cell dedifferentiation is
regulated through the NOX1–ADAM17 axis, which is a strong claim given that the only
evidence indicating an involvement of NOX1 is the upregulation of NOX1 mRNA upon
irradiation and IL-17A treatment, and the downregulation of NOX1 mRNA in irradiated
ADAM17fl/fl; Defa6-Cre mice. At a minimum, effects on NOX1 expression should be
confirmed at the protein level, ideally by immunostaining in mouse tissues. Additionally,
demonstrating reduced ROS production upon Paneth cell–specific IL-17RA knockout
(e.g., by ROS analysis in irradiated organoids using indicators such as CellROX or
H2DCFDA) would further strengthen the proposed link between IL-17RA signaling and
ROS-mediated ADAM17 activation. Even then, the title might falsely indicate regulation
by NOX1, as ROS might be increased by multiple other mechanisms upon irradiation.
Response: We stained and quantified NOX1 protein via immunohistochemistry in the
ilium of irradiated Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre+/- and Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-cre+/-. Protein data matched
expression data as we saw reduced NOX1 in both Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre+ and Il17rafl/fl;Defa6-
cre+ as compared to their cre- counter parts (Figs. S4B & S7G). We also updated our title and
removed NOX1 from it.
Comment: Regarding the title, I have an additional remark: the authors do not provide
direct evidence that the observed effect is specifically mediated by immune cell–derived
IL-17A. To be accurate, either immune cells should be removed from the title, or
experiments should be included to specifically address their involvement. Notably, IL-
17A can be expressed by other cell types, such as fibroblasts, as reported by Lotti et al.,
2013 (https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20131195).
Response: We have updated our title to remove any mention of immune derived IL-
17A. Furthermore, we specify the importance of IL-17RA signaling on Paneth
progenitors rather than IL-17A signaling.
Comment: As stated in the main text, ADAM17 is expressed in Paneth cells of both
naïve and irradiated mice (Fig. S5A). Based on the images, ADAM17 expression
appears to be considerably lower in irradiated mice compared to non-irradiated controls.
The authors neither comment on this nor provide further analysis of differential ADAM17
expression between the two conditions. If confirmed, this would contradict the results
shown in Figure 6H, where re-analysis of published scRNA-seq data from irradiated
mice indicated increased ADAM17 expression. This discrepancy should be addressed
and discussed.
Response: We have provided higher quality images in figure S5A.
Comment: Figure S6 is intended to show a Paneth cell–specific ADAM17 knockout;
however, ADAM17 expression also appears reduced in other epithelial cells. Here either
higher-quality images should be provided to clarify this or it should be commented on
why a Paneth cell–specific knockout might lead to a broader reduction of ADAM17
expression.
Response: We have provided higher quality images in figure S6.
Comment: Figure 6K shows a reduction of lineage tracing in NAC-treated mice. Is it
possible to assess ADAM17 activity in these mice? This would help to strengthen the
link between ROS production and ADAM17 activation.
Response: We performed ADAM17 activity assays from the tissue of these mice. We
observed a trend towards a decrease of ADAM17 activity in tissue from NAC treated
mice as compared to the H2O control cohort (Fig. S4C).
Comment: Regarding Figure 7F, Kempen et al. state that there is no difference in the
tight junction protein ZO-1 in ADAM17fl/fl;Defa6-Cre mice and conclude that ADAM17
limits damage in response to irradiation by promoting cellular proliferation rather than
modulating gut barrier proteins. However, based on the images provided in Figure 7F, it
appears that ZO-1 is absent in the crypts of Adam17fl/fl;Defa6-cre mice. The authors
should either reconsider their statement or provide additional data to support their
interpretation.
Response: We have quantified this data via mean fluorescence intensity using ImageJ.
We observed no differences (Fig. 7H).
Minor Comments
Comment: In Figure 1A and F, Figure 3A, Figure 5E, Figure 6M, Figure 7A, Figure S3A
it is not described what the arrows should indicate.
Response: We have updated figure legends to describe what arrows should indicate.
Comment: Y-axes in Figure 1A,, 3A, 5E, 6M, 7A, 7D should start from 0.
Response: We have updated figures to ensure they all start from 0.
Comment: It is not described how PCNA+ cells in Figure 3D and Figure 7D were
quantified (cells per crypt? How many crypts per mouse?)
Response: We have updated the y-axis of these figures to better describe how the
images were quantified (PCNA+ cells/crypt structure). Furthermore, all cell counts were
done on at least 30 crypts per mouse. This information has been added to the statistical
analysis section in the methods.
Comment: Authors should describe in more detail how outliers were identified and in
which experiments outliers were excluded.
Response: Outliers were determined by using GraphPad Prism (ROUT analysis, Q=1%). This
information has been included in the statistical analysis section in the methods.
Furthermore, figures in which outliers have been removed have been noted in figure
legends.
Comment: It is not always clear how many times the experiments were repeated or
how many samples were analyzed and quantified. For example, the authors state:
“Figures 5A, 5B, 5G, and 5I are representative of 2–3 mice. Figures 5B, 5D, 5E,
5G, and 5H are generated from 2–3 independent experiments, and representative
images are shown and quantified.” This level of reporting is insufficient for a high-quality journal
such as Nature Communications. The exact number of biological and technical
replicates, as well as the precise number of mice analyzed in each experiment, must be
clearly specified.
Response: The exact number of replicates, as well as the precise number of mice
analyzed in each experiment, has been clearly specified in figure legends.
Comment: The manuscript refers to Figure S6A, however, Figure S6 has no A or B.
Response: This discrepancy has been fixed in the manuscript.

### Reviewer 1

The authors have addressed all my concerns.

### Reviewer 2

Kempen et al. have performed substantial additional work and have considerably improved their manuscript. They addressed most of my previous suggestions and concerns, and the revisions have strengthened the overall quality and interpretability of the study.
However, two points still need to be clarified:
1. The age of the mice.
I appreciate that the authors included mouse ages in the figure legends. Unfortunately, it is not clear whether Cre+ and Cre- mice were age-matched or not. This is very critical, as previously the authors reported no difference of lysozyme expression in the intestinal epithelium of 6-week-old and a reduction of Paneth cell number in 10-week-old IL17RAfl/fl;Villin-cre mice (Lin et al., 2022 PMID: 35081371) and hence the age of the mice might substantially influence the outcome of some experiments. For example, in Figure 2E where the other show a reduction of Paneth cells, the figure legend indicates: “mice were 7.9, and 14.6 weeks old”. If these mice were not age-matched the authors cannot rule out that the mouse age influenced the outcome of the experiments. The same concern applies to Figure S1J, in which 6.7, 10 and 11.6 week old mice were used, and the number of Lyz1 positive cells in Cre+ mice show noticeable variation.
2. Interpretion of Figure S3C:
In Figure S3C, the authors examine whether treatment with IL-25 or IL-17C induces the formation of green Defa6-cre;mTmG mice organoids. For IL-25 they show a reduction from 7% to 0% composition between untreated and treated organoids. For IL-17C they show a rather drastic increase from 0% to more than 20%, which is comparable to the effect of IL-17A. Despite this the authors write:”Our results showed no significant increase in green organoid development from passaged Defa6-cre;mT/mG mice post-irradiation after IL-25 or IL-17C treatment (Fig. S3C)”. Which seems to me like a misinterpretation of the experiments. Additionally, the figure legend states: “There were 3 mice in each treatment group in figures S3C”. Yet, only one data point per group is shown in the graph. Can the authors elaborate on this discrepancy?
Minor point:
In Figure 6A, the authors show differences in secreted factors regulating Wnt and Notch ligands. They then state:
“Interestingly, Ly6a but not Ly6d, Anxa1, Anxa3, Anxa5, Yap, and Hbegf expression was increased in the small intestine of Cre+ mice as compared to Cre– mice (Fig. 6A & S4A).”
A) The authors should include the Wnt targets in the text.
B) They should also mention that the increased ligand expression does not appear to translate into a noticeable effect on downstream targets.
Additional typos:
• Line 1133: Should this be “3 experiments”?
• Figure S3A: “Defe6-cre” should be corrected to “Defa6-cre.”
